subtopic_detail: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis: ASHM 3-drug regimen
stem:
A 27-year-old intern sustains a hollow-bore needlestick injury while cannulating a patient known to have HIV with a detectable viral load of 42,000 copies/mL on an incomplete antiretroviral regimen. The exposure occurred 90 minutes ago. She squeezed the site, washed with soap and water, and presented immediately to the emergency department.

She is fit, on no regular medications, and has no personal history of hepatitis B or C. She is not pregnant, sexually active with one long-term partner using barrier contraception, and her last HIV test six months ago was negative. Baseline bloods including HIV serology, hepatitis serology, syphilis, renal function and pregnancy test are being drawn now.

The source patient is confirmed HIV-positive with resistance testing showing wild-type virus fully sensitive to first-line antiretrovirals. She reports no allergies. Local infectious diseases has been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Small puncture wound left index finger, minimal bleeding, no other injuries.
data_table.Investigations: Baseline HIV, hepatitis B/C, syphilis serology and pregnancy test collected; eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m^2.
data_table.Medications: Nil regular. No known drug allergies.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis to commence now?

options.text: Zidovudine plus lamivudine twice daily for 28 days
Efavirenz plus zidovudine-lamivudine daily for 28 days
Tenofovir disoproxil-emtricitabine daily for 28 days without a third agent
Tenofovir disoproxil-emtricitabine plus dolutegravir daily for 28 days
Await baseline source patient viral load and defer any prophylaxis for 48 hours

subtopic_detail: PJP primary prophylaxis at CD4 threshold
stem:
A 44-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV during a sexual health screen after a new partner tested positive. He is asymptomatic, has never taken antiretrovirals and has no prior AIDS-defining illness. He works full time and has no fevers, cough, weight loss or oral candidiasis.

On examination he looks well. Chest is clear and there is no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. There is no oral thrush and no skin lesions. His BMI is 26 kg/m^2 and there are no signs of wasting.

Initial staging bloods return the same day. Full blood count, renal function and liver function are within normal limits. CD4 count is 148 cells/microL, HIV RNA 84,000 copies/mL, HLA-B*5701 negative, hepatitis B and C serology negative, toxoplasma IgG negative, syphilis EIA negative. He has no sulfa drug allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Well, no oral thrush, chest clear, no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: CD4 148 cells/microL, HIV RNA 84,000 copies/mL, toxoplasma IgG negative, HLA-B*5701 negative, hepatitis B/C negative, eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m^2.

lead_in: In addition to commencing antiretroviral therapy, what is the most appropriate opportunistic infection prophylaxis?

options.text: Azithromycin 1200 mg orally once weekly
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg orally daily
Valganciclovir 900 mg orally daily
Fluconazole 200 mg orally weekly for cryptococcal prophylaxis
No opportunistic infection prophylaxis is required at this stage

subtopic_detail: First response to a detectable viral load after years of suppression
stem: A 41-year-old woman on antiretroviral therapy for four years, suppressed at every visit, attends for routine review and feels well. Two months ago she started shift work, and began esomeprazole and a calcium supplement bought over the counter.

data_table.Results: HIV RNA 3,400 copies per millilitre today; undetectable three and nine months ago
data_table.Examination: Well; weight stable; no thrush, rash or lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ask about missed doses and interacting medicines before changing
Switch her to a different antiretroviral combination at this visit
Add a fourth antiretroviral agent to the current regimen today
Stop all treatment until a resistance genotype result is available
Repeat the CD4 count alone and review her again in six months

subtopic_detail: Advanced HIV with CD4 <50: MAC evaluation and prophylaxis
stem:
A 51-year-old man with HIV, previously lost to follow up for four years, re-presents with six weeks of fevers, night sweats, drenching sweats and 8 kg unintentional weight loss. He is not on antiretroviral therapy. He denies cough or shortness of breath and has not travelled recently.

On examination he is thin with temporal wasting. Temperature 38.2 degrees C, pulse rate 104, blood pressure 108/68, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 percent on room air. There is oral candidiasis but no pulmonary crackles. The abdomen is soft with tender hepatomegaly to 4 cm below the costal margin. There is no focal lymphadenopathy or meningism.

Investigations return today: CD4 count 32 cells/microL, HIV RNA 380,000 copies/mL, haemoglobin 92 g/L (135-175), alkaline phosphatase 480 U/L (30-110), gamma-GT 210 U/L (5-50), bilirubin within normal limits, chest x-ray clear, blood cultures still pending. Cryptococcal antigen is negative and tuberculin gamma-release assay is negative. Sputum acid-fast smear is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2 C, HR 104, BP 108/68, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent room air.
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, oral thrush, tender hepatomegaly 4 cm, chest clear.
data_table.Investigations: CD4 32 cells/microL, HIV RNA 380,000 copies/mL, Hb 92 g/L (135-175), ALP 480 U/L (30-110), GGT 210 U/L (5-50), CXR clear, cryptococcal antigen negative, QuantiFERON negative, sputum AFB smear negative.
data_table.Medications: Nil. Not on antiretrovirals for four years.

lead_in: In addition to starting antiretroviral therapy and PJP prophylaxis, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence azithromycin 1200 mg orally weekly for MAC primary prophylaxis without further investigation
Add oral fluconazole 400 mg daily empirically for suspected disseminated cryptococcosis
Empirical four-drug antituberculous therapy pending culture results
Start valganciclovir empirically for suspected CMV disease
Send mycobacterial blood cultures before considering MAC prophylaxis or treatment

subtopic_detail: AIDS-defining CNS lesion: toxoplasmosis vs primary CNS lymphoma
stem:
A 39-year-old woman with poorly adherent HIV presents with a two-week history of progressive right-sided weakness, headaches and one episode of a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure. She stopped her antiretrovirals six months ago and has not been engaged in specialist care.

On examination she is afebrile with right hemiparesis, right-sided pronator drift and mild expressive dysphasia. There is no meningism, papilloedema or rash. Cardiorespiratory and abdominal examinations are unremarkable.

CD4 count is 42 cells/microL, HIV RNA 220,000 copies/mL, toxoplasma IgG positive, cryptococcal antigen negative and syphilis serology negative. She is not on any PJP or toxoplasmosis prophylaxis. MRI brain with contrast shows two ring-enhancing lesions, one in the left basal ganglia and one at the grey-white junction of the right frontal lobe, each with surrounding oedema. She has no sulfa allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Right hemiparesis, right pronator drift, mild expressive dysphasia, no meningism.
data_table.Investigations: CD4 42 cells/microL, HIV RNA 220,000 copies/mL, toxoplasma IgG positive, cryptococcal antigen negative, MRI brain: two ring-enhancing lesions with oedema.
data_table.Medications: Nil currently. No PJP/toxo prophylaxis. No sulfa allergy.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Empirical sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine and folinic acid, reassessed at 10 to 14 days
Proceed directly to stereotactic brain biopsy before commencing any antimicrobial therapy
Commence liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine induction
Start high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone before any antimicrobial therapy
Immediate whole-brain radiotherapy for presumed primary CNS lymphoma

subtopic_detail: Initial ART regimen selection per ASHM 2024
stem:
A 32-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with HIV during antenatal-planning bloods; she is not currently pregnant but plans to conceive within the next six months with her HIV-negative male partner. She has no prior antiretroviral exposure and is otherwise well.

On examination she is well with a BMI of 24 kg/m^2. There is no oral candidiasis, no lymphadenopathy and no skin lesions. Cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examinations are unremarkable.

Baseline investigations show CD4 count 460 cells/microL, HIV RNA 68,000 copies/mL, HLA-B*5701 negative, hepatitis B surface antigen negative with immune serology (positive surface antibody), hepatitis C antibody negative, syphilis serology negative and rubella immune. Renal function, liver function and lipids are within normal limits. She has no known drug allergies and takes no regular medications. She has been counselled about U=U (undetectable equals untransmittable) and preconception planning.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Well, no oral thrush, no lymphadenopathy.
data_table.Investigations: CD4 460 cells/microL, HIV RNA 68,000 copies/mL, HLA-B*5701 negative, HBsAg negative (immune), HCV negative, eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m^2, LFTs and lipids within normal limits.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antiretroviral regimen?

options.text: Zidovudine, lamivudine and nevirapine three times daily
Efavirenz with tenofovir disoproxil and emtricitabine as a single daily tablet
Ritonavir-boosted atazanavir with tenofovir disoproxil and emtricitabine
Bictegravir with tenofovir alafenamide and emtricitabine as a single daily tablet
Long-acting injectable cabotegravir and rilpivirine every two months as initial therapy

subtopic_detail: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) after ART initiation
stem:
A 46-year-old man was diagnosed with HIV three weeks ago after presenting with a two-month history of low-grade fevers, weight loss and a productive cough. Chest imaging at that presentation showed patchy right upper lobe changes; QuantiFERON was positive and a sputum GeneXpert confirmed rifampicin-sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis. He was commenced on isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol two weeks ago, and integrase inhibitor based antiretroviral therapy was started one week ago at his baseline CD4 count of 48 cells/microL and HIV RNA of 620,000 copies/mL.

He now re-presents with worsening fevers to 39.1 degrees C, new painful right supraclavicular and cervical lymphadenopathy, increased cough and pleuritic chest pain. Chest x-ray shows enlarging right upper lobe consolidation and new right paratracheal lymphadenopathy compared with imaging from three weeks ago. He is adherent with both regimens and denies missed doses.

Repeat sputum acid-fast smear is negative and there is no evidence of drug-resistant tuberculosis on repeat susceptibility testing. Blood cultures are negative to date. He is haemodynamically stable, saturating 96 percent on room air.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1 C, HR 108, BP 122/78, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent room air.
data_table.Examination: Tender right supraclavicular and cervical lymphadenopathy, right basal crackles.
data_table.Investigations: CXR: enlarging RUL consolidation, new right paratracheal nodes. Sputum AFB smear negative. Blood cultures negative. Susceptibility unchanged.
data_table.Medications: RIPE therapy day 14. INSTI-based ART day 7. Adherent.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step?

options.text: Stop antiretroviral therapy and continue antituberculous therapy alone
Change antituberculous therapy to a second-line regimen for suspected multi-drug resistant tuberculosis
Continue both regimens and commence prednisolone 1.5 mg/kg daily for two weeks with a taper
Add broad-spectrum intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam for presumed bacterial superinfection
Excisional biopsy of the enlarged supraclavicular node before any further treatment change

subtopic_detail: PrEP eligibility and baseline monitoring per ASHM
stem:
A 29-year-old man attends a sexual health clinic requesting HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis. He is HIV negative and has had condomless receptive anal intercourse with multiple male partners over the last six months, including one partner recently diagnosed with rectal gonorrhoea. He describes occasional crystal methamphetamine use in sexual contexts.

He is otherwise well with no significant medical history and takes no regular medications. He mentions that four days ago he had a condom failure with an anonymous partner of unknown HIV status. He denies any current fevers, rash, sore throat or lymphadenopathy.

On examination he looks well with normal vital signs. There is no oral thrush, no lymphadenopathy and no rash. Baseline point-of-care fourth-generation HIV antigen-antibody test is negative today. Serum creatinine drawn last week was 78 micromol/L (60-110) with an eGFR greater than 90 mL/min/1.73m^2. Hepatitis B surface antigen was negative with immune surface antibody, and hepatitis C antibody was negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Well, no oral thrush, no lymphadenopathy, no rash.
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care 4th-gen HIV Ag/Ab negative today; creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m^2; HBsAg negative (immune); HCV negative.
data_table.Medications: Nil regular. No known drug allergies.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence a 28-day PEP course now, then transition to daily PrEP once repeat HIV serology at four weeks is negative
Commence daily tenofovir disoproxil-emtricitabine PrEP today and arrange three-monthly review
Send fourth-generation HIV antigen-antibody test plus HIV RNA today and defer PrEP until results confirm HIV-negative status
Recommend consistent condom use and STI screening only, without offering PrEP given his methamphetamine use
Commence on-demand event-driven PrEP dosing (2-1-1) as first-line strategy without further HIV testing

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated cystitis in a non-pregnant woman
stem:
A 28-year-old woman presents to a suburban general practice with two days of dysuria, urinary frequency and suprapubic discomfort. She has never had a urinary tract infection before, is not sexually active in the past three months and takes no regular medications. She uses reliable contraception, her last menstrual period was 10 days ago, and a bedside urine beta-hCG is negative. She has no fever, flank pain, vomiting or vaginal discharge.

Examination reveals a comfortable woman with mild suprapubic tenderness. Bedside urinalysis is positive for nitrites and leucocyte esterase, negative for blood. She reports no penicillin, sulfonamide or nitrofuran allergy, and her estimated GFR at a recent workplace medical was above 60 mL/min/1.73m^2.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99 percent room air, T 36.8 C.
data_table.Examination: Mild suprapubic tenderness, no flank tenderness, no vaginal discharge on external inspection.
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis nitrites positive, leucocyte esterase positive, blood negative. Urine beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical oral antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Amoxicillin 500 mg orally every 8 hours for 5 days
Cefalexin 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 5 days
Trimethoprim 300 mg orally once daily for 3 days
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 3 days
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally every 6 hours for 3 days

subtopic_detail: Acute pyelonephritis - oral versus IV thresholds
stem:
A 34-year-old woman presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 24 hours of right flank pain, rigors and vomiting on a background of two days of dysuria and frequency. She is not pregnant (urine beta-hCG negative), has no structural urinary tract abnormality, no indwelling catheter and no recent antibiotic exposure. She has taken oral fluids overnight and passed urine twice this morning.

On examination she is uncomfortable but alert and cooperative. There is right renal angle tenderness and no suprapubic mass. Vitals: HR 102, BP 118/74, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent room air, T 38.6 C. Bedside bloods show WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 96 mg/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L (baseline 72), lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Blood and urine cultures have been sent. She has no vomiting since arrival, tolerated 200 mL of oral fluid and has no allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 118/74, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent, T 38.6 C.
data_table.Examination: Right renal angle tenderness, no suprapubic mass, no vaginal discharge.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 96 mg/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L (baseline 72), lactate 1.4 mmol/L, urinalysis nitrites and leucocytes positive.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg loading
IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg single dose then oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily
Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg every 6 hours for 14 days total
Oral cefalexin 500 mg every 6 hours for 14 days total
Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 12 hours for 7 to 10 days

subtopic_detail: Catheter-associated bacteriuria - when to treat
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 78-year-old man on the rehabilitation ward six weeks after a right total hip replacement. He has an indwelling urinary catheter placed intraoperatively for peri-operative retention that has remained in situ due to ongoing voiding trials.

The nursing team sent a routine mid-stream catheter specimen this morning that has just returned: greater than 10^5 CFU/mL Escherichia coli, sensitive to trimethoprim, amoxicillin-clavulanate and cefalexin. He is afebrile, feels well, is eating and mobilising with physiotherapy, and has no suprapubic pain, flank tenderness, delirium or new confusion. Vital signs are within normal limits and his most recent bloods 48 hours ago showed WCC 7.1 x10^9/L, CRP 8 mg/L and creatinine 82 micromol/L (baseline 78). His trial of void is planned for tomorrow morning.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Well, afebrile, no suprapubic or flank tenderness, no delirium.
data_table.Investigations: Catheter urine culture E. coli greater than 10^5 CFU/mL sensitive to trimethoprim, cefalexin, augmentin. WCC 7.1 x10^9/L, CRP 8 mg/L 48 h ago.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 7 days empirically
Commence oral cefalexin 500 mg 12-hourly for 5 days empirically
Change the catheter and commence trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 7 days
No antibiotics and proceed with the planned trial of void tomorrow
Send blood cultures and start IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily pending sensitivities

subtopic_detail: UTI in pregnancy - agent selection by gestation
stem:
A 32-year-old primigravida at 38 weeks and 2 days gestation presents to her GP with two days of dysuria and urinary frequency. She has no fever, flank pain, uterine tenderness, contractions, per-vaginal loss or reduced fetal movements. Her antenatal course has been uncomplicated, her group B streptococcus swab at 36 weeks was negative, and she has no penicillin, sulfonamide or nitrofuran allergy.

Examination is unremarkable with a soft non-tender uterus, cephalic presentation, fetal heart rate 142 bpm and normal maternal vitals. Bedside urinalysis is positive for nitrites and leucocytes. A midstream urine sample has been sent for culture. She is booked for a routine antenatal review in one week and has no immediate delivery plan.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits; fetal HR 142 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus, cephalic, no PV loss.
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis nitrites positive, leucocytes positive. MSU sent for culture. GBS swab negative at 36 weeks.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical oral antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Cefalexin 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 5 days
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally every 6 hours for 5 days
Trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 3 days
Amoxicillin 500 mg orally every 8 hours for 5 days
Norfloxacin 400 mg orally every 12 hours for 3 days

subtopic_detail: Recurrent UTI - continuous prophylaxis threshold
stem:
A 42-year-old woman attends her GP for review of recurrent uncomplicated cystitis. Over the past 12 months she has had four culture-confirmed episodes, all growing E. coli sensitive to trimethoprim and nitrofurantoin, each responding promptly to a 5-day course. Between episodes she is entirely well.

She is post-menopausal since 40 following bilateral oophorectomy for BRCA1 mutation, is not on hormone therapy, and reports no vaginal dryness or dyspareunia currently. She has had a renal tract ultrasound (normal), a post-void residual scan (12 mL) and a cystoscopy performed by a urologist (normal). She drinks 2 L of fluid daily, voids post-coitally and does not use spermicides. Behavioural and hydration measures have not reduced her episode frequency. She has no penicillin, sulfa or nitrofuran allergy, eGFR is above 60 mL/min/1.73m^2 and she is not planning pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: No suprapubic or flank tenderness.
data_table.Investigations: Renal tract ultrasound normal, PVR 12 mL, cystoscopy normal, eGFR above 60.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continuous nitrofurantoin 50 mg orally nocte for 6 months
Post-coital single-dose trimethoprim 150 mg after each episode of intercourse
Self-initiated stand-by short-course trimethoprim at symptom onset
CT urogram to exclude urolithiasis and upper tract lesions
Cranberry supplements 500 mg twice daily for 6 months as prophylaxis

subtopic_detail: Complicated UTI in a man - workup priority
stem:
A 58-year-old man presents to his GP with a 5-day history of dysuria, urinary hesitancy and perineal ache. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin (HbA1c 51 mmol/mol) and mild lower urinary tract symptoms attributed to benign prostatic hyperplasia but is not on any prostate medication. He has not previously had a urinary tract infection.

Examination reveals a mildly tender lower abdomen. Digital rectal examination discloses a smooth, exquisitely tender prostate. He is afebrile with normal vital signs. Bedside urinalysis is positive for nitrites and leucocytes. A mid-stream urine has been sent. He has no penicillin, sulfonamide or fluoroquinolone allergy and eGFR is 78 mL/min/1.73m^2.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Mild lower abdominal tenderness; DRE reveals a smooth, exquisitely tender prostate.
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis nitrites and leucocytes positive; MSU sent; eGFR 78; HbA1c 51 mmol/mol.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical oral antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally every 6 hours for 7 days
Trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 5 days empirically
Cefalexin 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days
Trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 14 days empirically

subtopic_detail: Severe pyelonephritis with sepsis - source control priority
stem:
A 66-year-old woman presents to a regional emergency department with a 12-hour history of rigors, right flank pain and vomiting. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin and had a left ureteric stone treated with ureteroscopy and stent insertion three weeks ago. The stent remains in situ. She last passed urine four hours ago and has produced 20 mL in a bedpan since arrival 90 minutes ago.

She is confused with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 13. Vital signs: HR 128, BP 82/48 (unchanged after 1 L crystalloid), RR 28, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs, T 39.4 C. Examination reveals right renal angle tenderness and mottled peripheries. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.28, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L. WCC 18.6 x10^9/L, creatinine 214 micromol/L (baseline 74), CRP 288 mg/L. Blood and urine cultures have been drawn and IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g plus a single dose of gentamicin have been given. A bedside renal ultrasound shows right-sided hydronephrosis with a dilated ureter above the retained stent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 82/48 (unchanged after 1 L fluid), RR 28, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L, T 39.4 C.
data_table.Examination: GCS 13, confused, mottled peripheries, right renal angle tenderness.
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.28, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, WCC 18.6 x10^9/L, creatinine 214 micromol/L (baseline 74), CRP 288 mg/L. Renal ultrasound: right hydronephrosis above retained ureteric stent.

lead_in: In addition to ongoing fluid resuscitation and vasopressor support, what is the most important next intervention?

options.text: Add IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose to broaden gram-positive cover empirically
Urgent urology referral for nephrostomy or stent exchange to decompress the obstruction
CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast to define the obstruction before intervention
IV hydrocortisone 200 mg daily as an early adjunct for relative adrenal insufficiency
Insert a urethral catheter to monitor hourly urine output and reassess in one hour

subtopic_detail: Asymptomatic bacteriuria pre-urological procedure
stem:
You are the on-call medical registrar asked to review a 74-year-old man booked for elective transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) tomorrow morning. He is being admitted overnight for pre-operative optimisation. He takes ramipril for hypertension and has no allergies.

As part of routine pre-operative screening, his midstream urine collected in clinic yesterday has returned this evening growing greater than 10^5 CFU/mL Enterococcus faecalis, susceptible to amoxicillin and vancomycin. He is asymptomatic - no dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain, flank pain or fever. He does not have an indwelling catheter. His inflammatory markers, renal function and vital signs are within normal limits, and he is not immunosuppressed or pregnant (male). The urology team has asked for your input on antibiotics before he goes to theatre.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Asymptomatic, no suprapubic or flank tenderness, no catheter.
data_table.Investigations: Preoperative MSU: Enterococcus faecalis greater than 10^5 CFU/mL, susceptible to amoxicillin and vancomycin. WCC, CRP, creatinine within normal limits.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Proceed to surgery with the standard cefazolin skin-prophylaxis dose at induction only
Defer surgery indefinitely until repeat urine cultures are sterile on two occasions
Give a single dose of oral amoxicillin 1 g at the time of surgery only, no other cover
Give targeted IV amoxicillin 2 g at induction with a short peri-operative course
Give IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg at induction to broaden enterococcal cover empirically

subtopic_detail: Warfarin reversal high INR no bleed
stem:
A 68-year-old man on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve presents with a routine INR check showing 8.4. He has no bleeding, no bruising, and reports no recent medication changes but did complete a 5 day course of clarithromycin last week for a chest infection. His last INR 3 weeks ago was 2.6.

He is haemodynamically stable and fully asymptomatic. His usual warfarin dose is 4 mg daily. There is no easy bruising on skin examination, no gastrointestinal bleeding, and no haematuria.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 138/82, RR 14, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 36.6 C
data_table.Investigations: INR 8.4 today (was 2.6 three weeks ago); Hb 138 g/L (130-170); platelets 264 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110)
data_table.Medications: Warfarin 4 mg daily; recent 5 day clarithromycin course completed last week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Withhold warfarin only and recheck INR in 24 hours without vitamin K with cardiac monitoring throughout
Withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) 1 to 2 mg with cardiac monitoring throughout
Withhold warfarin and give prothrombin complex concentrate (Prothrombinex-VF) 25 IU per kg IV
Withhold warfarin and give vitamin K1 10 mg intravenously slowly with cardiac monitoring throughout
Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL per kg intravenously over 30 minutes with cardiac monitoring throughout

subtopic_detail: Type B dissection BP control
stem:
A 58-year-old man presents with 2 hours of sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to his back and left arm. CT aortogram confirms an acute type B (descending) aortic dissection extending from just distal to the left subclavian to the infra-renal aorta. He is haemodynamically stable with no end-organ malperfusion.

On examination he has equal radial pulses, no focal neurology, and no abdominal pain. Renal function is normal, urine output preserved, and there is no leg ischaemia. He has a normal chest examination.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 178/98 (right arm) 176/96 (left arm), RR 18, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Investigations: Troponin 12 ng/L (<14); creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110); Hb 138 g/L (130-170); D-dimer 4200 ng/mL
data_table.Imaging: CT aortogram: acute type B dissection from left subclavian to infra-renal aorta; no malperfusion; no rupture; no pericardial effusion

lead_in: What are the target heart rate and systolic blood pressure over the next 20 minutes?

options.text: Heart rate under 60 and systolic BP under 140 mmHg using metoprolol 5 mg IV single dose only
Heart rate under 100 and systolic BP under 160 mmHg using IV GTN monotherapy
Heart rate under 60 and systolic BP under 100 mmHg using nifedipine IR sublingual
No BP target - proceed straight to endovascular repair (TEVAR) with cardiac monitoring throughout
Heart rate under 60 and systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg using IV esmolol or labetalol first

subtopic_detail: MTP activation criteria
stem:
A 44-year-old man is brought in by ambulance after being struck by a car. He has an obvious pelvic fracture and blood at the meatus. Prehospital he has received 1 L of crystalloid and 1 unit of O-negative packed red cells.

On arrival he is peripherally shut down with cold pale extremities. Abdomen is distended and tender. FAST scan shows free fluid in the abdomen. Ongoing bleeding is estimated at 250 mL per 5 minutes based on his chest drain and pelvic external stabiliser output. His last recorded systolic pressure was 78 despite ongoing resuscitation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, BP 78/44, RR 32, SpO2 96 percent on non-rebreather, temp 35.2 C
data_table.Investigations: Hb 68 g/L (130-170); platelets 92 x10^9/L (150-400); INR 1.8 (0.9-1.2); fibrinogen 1.4 g/L (2-4); pH 7.18, base excess -12, lactate 9.4 mmol/L, ionised calcium 0.92 mmol/L (1.10-1.30)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Withhold platelets until count drops below 50 x10^9/L and give red cells only
Transfuse further packed red cells only until Hb is over 100, then reassess coagulation
Prothrombin complex concentrate (Prothrombinex-VF) 50 IU per kg IV as the first blood product
Activate the massive transfusion protocol with 1:1:1 packed red cells, FFP, and platelets
Recombinant factor VIIa 90 mcg per kg IV as first-line for uncontrolled haemorrhage

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis vs cellulitis
stem:
A 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to your ED with 24 hours of pain out of proportion to physical findings in his right calf. The skin over the area looks like mild cellulitis with faint erythema. He is systemically unwell.

On examination there is faint erythema over the medial calf, exquisite tenderness on light palpation extending well beyond the area of erythema, a small area of dusky skin at the medial malleolus, and reduced sensation over the medial ankle. There is no wound of entry visible. Pedal pulses are palpable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122, BP 96/58, RR 26, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temp 38.7 C
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 260 mg/L (<5); sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145); glucose 16.8 mmol/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110); Hb 118 g/L (130-170); lactate 4.2 mmol/L
data_table.Imaging: Bedside soft tissue ultrasound shows fascial thickening and small gas bubbles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: IV flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours and elevate the limb, review at 4 hours
Urgent surgical exploration with debridement plus empirical IV meropenem plus clindamycin
IV ceftriaxone plus metronidazole and MRI to confirm before considering surgery
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy first, then antibiotics and involve senior review
Bedside incision and drainage at the point of maximal tenderness and admission for observation

subtopic_detail: Type A dissection surgical
stem:
A 46-year-old man with a family history of connective tissue disease presents with sudden tearing chest pain radiating between the shoulder blades. He is normotensive but pale and diaphoretic. CT aortogram shows an intimal flap involving the ascending aorta extending into the descending aorta with a small pericardial effusion measuring 8 mm.

On examination his right radial pulse is diminished compared to the left and there is a diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. He has no focal neurology and no leg ischaemia. Bedside echocardiogram shows no tamponade physiology but confirms the pericardial fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 118/68 (right arm) 138/80 (left arm), RR 22, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Investigations: Troponin 12 ng/L (<14); creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110); Hb 132 g/L (130-170); D-dimer 6800 ng/mL
data_table.Imaging: CT aortogram: intimal flap from just above aortic root into descending aorta; 8 mm pericardial effusion; no rupture; visible root involvement
data_table.Echo: Aortic regurgitation moderate; pericardial fluid 8 mm without tamponade

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate cardiothoracic surgical repair of the ascending aorta with cardiac monitoring
Medical management with IV labetalol and IV nitroprusside targeting SBP 100 to 120 mmHg
Thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) as first-line with cardiac monitoring in place
Emergency pericardiocentesis and admit to CCU on IV nitrate infusion with cardiac monitoring
Aspirin 300 mg plus ticagrelor 180 mg for presumed acute coronary syndrome

subtopic_detail: Sepsis hour-1 bundle
stem:
A 74-year-old woman is admitted from a nursing home with 24 hours of confusion, fever and reduced urine output. She has a chronic indwelling urinary catheter for outlet obstruction. She is on metformin for diabetes and no other regular medications.

On examination she is drowsy, has warm peripheries with a wide pulse pressure, and mottling of her thighs. Her catheter bag has cloudy foul-smelling urine. Chest is clear and abdomen is soft with suprapubic tenderness. She weighs approximately 60 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118 sinus tachycardia, BP 88/38, RR 26, SpO2 96 percent on 2 L nasal prongs, temp 39.4 C
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.6 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 320 mg/L (<5); creatinine 218 micromol/L (baseline 78; 60-110); urea 18 mmol/L (2.5-7.5); lactate 4.6 mmol/L (<2); glucose 12.4 mmol/L; VBG pH 7.28; procalcitonin pending
data_table.Catheter urine: Cloudy foul-smelling; leucocyte esterase positive; nitrite positive; microscopy pending

lead_in: What is the correct sequence of actions in the first hour?

options.text: IV normal saline 30 mL per kg over 3 hours, wait for cultures before antibiotics
Blood cultures, arterial or venous lactate, then IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g
Empirical IV ceftriaxone 1 g plus oral metronidazole and 500 mL saline bolus, review in 6 hours
Vasopressor infusion first via peripheral IV, then antibiotics, then cultures
Broad-spectrum antibiotics alone (piperacillin-tazobactam) without cultures, IV fluids or vasopressor

subtopic_detail: LV free wall rupture post-MI
stem:
A 68-year-old woman who presented 6 days ago with an anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI is on the coronary care unit. She has been mobilising well since day 3. At 4 am the nurse calls you because she suddenly becomes short of breath and hypotensive.

On arrival she looks unwell, has muffled heart sounds and is peripherally shut down. Jugular venous pressure is grossly elevated with y-descent absent. Bedside echocardiogram shows a large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse. There is no new ST-segment shift on ECG and CXR shows a modest widening of the cardiac silhouette compared with the film from 24 hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 68/40, RR 30, SpO2 92 percent on 15 L non-rebreather, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Investigations: Troponin 8200 ng/L (on downtrend from admission peak 45 000); Hb 96 g/L (was 118 yesterday); creatinine 108 micromol/L; INR 1.1; lactate 5.8 mmol/L; ECG anterior Q waves, no new ST shift
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg; ticagrelor 90 mg BD; atorvastatin 80 mg; ramipril 5 mg; bisoprolol 5 mg
data_table.Echo: Large pericardial effusion with RV diastolic collapse; regional wall motion abnormalities consistent with old anterior infarct; no ventricular septal defect visualised

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?

options.text: Recurrent stent thrombosis - repeat coronary angiography and PCI and repeat as clinically indicated
Dressler syndrome - high dose aspirin and NSAIDs with colchicine, admit for observation and involve senior review
Post-MI ventricular septal defect - emergency surgery after intra-aortic balloon pump insertion
Papillary muscle rupture - emergency mitral valve surgery and repeat as clinically indicated
Left ventricular free wall rupture with cardiac tamponade - emergency cardiac surgery for pericardial evacuation

subtopic_detail: Warfarin reversal in life-threatening bleeding
stem:
A 72-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation with a CHA2DS2-VA of 4 presents to your regional emergency department with 2 hours of a sudden severe headache with vomiting and left sided weakness. He last took his warfarin 12 hours ago. He has no history of hepatic impairment. He usually runs an INR between 2.0 and 3.0.

On arrival he is GCS 12 with dysarthria, a left facial droop, and left arm 3/5 power. A non-contrast CT head confirms a 5 cm right basal ganglia intracerebral haemorrhage with 4 mm of midline shift. Blood pressure is 178/104 and haemodynamics are otherwise stable. IV access has been secured. He is nil by mouth pending neurosurgery review.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82 irregular, BP 178/104, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 36.8 C, GCS 12
data_table.Examination: Alert to voice; dysarthria; left facial droop; left arm 3/5 power; leg 4/5; no meningism; pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: INR 3.2; APTT 42 seconds; haemoglobin 132 g/L; platelets 220 x10^9/L; fibrinogen 3.4 g/L; sodium 140 potassium 4.2 creatinine 96; CT head as described

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal regimen?

options.text: Vitamin K 10 milligrams intravenously alone with hourly INR monitoring for the next 4 hours before considering further reversal treatment
Prothrombinex-VF 50 international units per kilogram intravenously plus vitamin K 5 to 10 milligrams intravenously with repeat INR at 30 minutes
Fresh frozen plasma 15 millilitres per kilogram alone without prothrombinex and vitamin K 1 milligram orally with repeat INR at 6 hours
Recombinant factor VIIa 90 micrograms per kilogram intravenously as the primary reversal agent given the intracranial haemorrhage
Idarucizumab 5 grams intravenously in two 2.5 gram doses as immediate specific reversal agent for the anticoagulant effect

subtopic_detail: Sepsis hour-1 bundle sequencing
stem:
A 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease stage 3 presents to your district hospital emergency department with 2 days of increasing dysuria, frank haematuria, and 6 hours of rigors. She had a right ureteric stent placed 3 weeks ago for an obstructing stone. She has been drinking 3 litres of water daily.

On arrival she is drowsy but rousable and haemodynamically compromised. Her right renal angle is tender. There is no rash. IV access has been secured with an 18 gauge cannula. The nurse has just returned from taking blood cultures and a serum lactate. Vital signs and gas results have just come back.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 84/48 (MAP 60), RR 28, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 38.9 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; mottled peripheries with capillary refill 4 seconds; right renal angle tender; abdomen soft; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pH 7.28 lactate 4.6 mmol/L base excess -8; white cell count 21 x10^9/L neutrophils 18; creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 130); urinalysis nitrites and leucocytes positive; bedside urine microscopy pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give a 30 millilitre per kilogram Hartmann's bolus over 30 minutes and commence peripheral noradrenaline 10 micrograms per minute immediately before starting antibiotics
Give a 30 millilitre per kilogram crystalloid bolus over 3 hours first then administer intravenous ceftriaxone 2 grams once the bolus is completed
Give intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 grams plus gentamicin 5 milligrams per kilogram now followed by a 30 millilitre per kilogram crystalloid bolus over 3 hours
Arrange urgent CT KUB and defer antibiotic administration until obstruction is confirmed and urology has assessed for immediate stent revision
Give intravenous meropenem 1 gram as monotherapy and 500 millilitres of Hartmann's bolus over 30 minutes before repeat vital signs assessment at 1 hour

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis first-line agent selection
stem:
A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman is referred to your general medicine outpatient clinic for review after a low-trauma right distal radius fracture 6 weeks ago after tripping on a garden hose. She takes ramipril 5 mg daily for hypertension and has no other medical history. She has no history of oesophageal disease and swallows tablets easily.

Her dual energy X-ray absorptiometry scan (DXA) at the femoral neck shows a T score of -2.9 and at lumbar spine -2.6. Her serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 62 nmol/L and corrected calcium is 2.32 mmol/L. Renal function is normal with an eGFR of 78 mL/min/1.73 m2. She is willing to accept an oral therapy and lives with her husband who can help her with dosing.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72, BP 132/78, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; well healed distal radius fracture with plaster removed 2 weeks ago; no proximal myopathy or bone tenderness elsewhere; no dental disease
data_table.Investigations: DXA femoral neck T -2.9 lumbar spine T -2.6; 25-OH-vitamin D 62 nmol/L; corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L; creatinine 68 eGFR 78; TSH 2.4 mIU/L; alkaline phosphatase 92 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Oral strontium ranelate 2 grams daily dissolved in water at bedtime with attention to cardiovascular risk factors and periodic cardiovascular review
Subcutaneous denosumab 60 milligrams every 6 months as first-line with strict adherence to schedule to avoid rebound bone loss on discontinuation
Subcutaneous teriparatide 20 micrograms daily for up to 24 months as anabolic therapy given the low T score at both femoral neck and lumbar spine
Oral alendronate 70 milligrams weekly with instructions to remain upright for 30 minutes after each dose and take vitamin D 1000 international units daily
Oral raloxifene 60 milligrams daily as a selective oestrogen receptor modulator with attention to hot flushes and venous thromboembolism risk

subtopic_detail: Aortic dissection type discrimination and initial management
stem:
A 58-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension presents to your metropolitan emergency department with sudden onset of tearing interscapular chest pain radiating to his back 60 minutes ago. He is a current smoker and has a strong family history of aortic aneurysm. He denies syncope. His pulses are palpable in both radial arteries with a difference in blood pressure of 24 mmHg between arms.

On arrival he is diaphoretic and anxious. Cardiovascular examination reveals an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge and equal bilateral chest expansion with air entry. There is no focal neurology or abdominal pain. IV access has been secured. A CT angiogram of the aorta has just returned and shows an intimal flap starting at the ascending aorta and extending distally past the arch into the descending thoracic aorta and abdominal aorta beyond the coeliac axis, without extension into the coronary ostia or a pericardial effusion.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 176/98 right arm and 152/86 left arm, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic; anxious; early diastolic murmur at left sternal edge; equal bilateral chest expansion; abdomen soft; distal pulses palpable and equal
data_table.Investigations: 12-lead ECG shows LV hypertrophy without ischaemic change; troponin negative; chest X-ray widened mediastinum; CT aortogram as described in stem

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous esmolol infusion titrated to heart rate under 60 followed by intravenous sodium nitroprusside to systolic under 120 mmHg with cardiothoracic referral
Intravenous labetalol 20 milligrams bolus and admit under vascular for medical management alone as this is a Stanford type B dissection amenable to conservative therapy
Thrombolysis with tenecteplase weight-based dosing intravenously for presumed anterior STEMI with new murmur suggestive of papillary muscle rupture
Intravenous morphine and oral aspirin 300 milligrams then clopidogrel 300 milligrams with admission to coronary care unit for further workup and troponin trending
Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to systolic blood pressure under 140 with intravenous furosemide 40 milligrams for the diastolic murmur suggestive of acute aortic regurgitation

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis recognition and management
stem:
A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and obesity presents to your regional emergency department with 24 hours of increasing right calf pain that has become disproportionate to the clinical findings. He recalled scratching his leg on garden wire 4 days ago. His pain has escalated despite oral paracetamol and now feels excruciating on light touch.

On examination there is a small area of erythema on the anterior right calf with hazy dusky discoloration extending beyond the erythematous border and a single haemorrhagic bulla. Sensation over the affected area is reduced. He has palpable pedal pulses and no obvious crepitus. He is drowsy and diaphoretic with cool peripheries. IV access has been secured and initial resuscitation has commenced with fluids and cultures drawn.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 96/58 (MAP 71), RR 26, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 38.6 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; cool peripheries with capillary refill 3 seconds; right calf with area of erythema, dusky discoloration beyond the erythematous border, one haemorrhagic bulla, reduced sensation, no crepitus; palpable pedal pulses; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 22 x10^9/L; sodium 132 potassium 4.4 creatinine 148 (baseline 90) urea 12; glucose 18.2 mmol/L; venous gas pH 7.28 lactate 4.4; CRP 380 mg/L; haemoglobin 128 g/L; LRINEC score 8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the lower limb to confirm gas in the tissue planes before any surgical review is arranged
Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 grams 6 hourly and mark the erythema border with observation for 4 hours before deciding on surgical review or escalation
Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 grams and elevate the limb with strict bed rest for cellulitis treatment while awaiting orthopaedic surgical review the next morning
Immediate surgical review with plan for urgent theatre debridement plus intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus clindamycin as empirical antibiotic cover
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy with 100 percent oxygen at 2.4 atmospheres for 90 minutes as adjunctive treatment before the first surgical debridement is performed

subtopic_detail: Adult anaphylaxis refractory to first-line adrenaline
stem:
A 62-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis attends an infusion suite for her scheduled infliximab infusion. She takes metoprolol 100 mg twice daily for chronic atrial fibrillation with a controlled rate. Within 10 minutes of starting the infusion she develops generalised urticaria, wheeze, and hypotension.

The infusion has been stopped, she has been laid flat, and she has received one dose of intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms into the anterolateral thigh. Five minutes later she remains hypotensive with persistent wheeze and hoarse voice. She has just received a second dose of intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms. She has IV access with two large-bore cannulae. She has been given 1 litre of Hartmann's solution over the last 5 minutes and is on 6 L/min via Hudson mask.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 82/48 (MAP 60), RR 28, SpO2 92% on 6 L/min via Hudson mask, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria; audible wheeze; hoarse voice; cool peripheries with capillary refill 3 seconds; alert
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pH 7.30 lactate 3.4 mmol/L; ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular response at 82

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Third intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms and continue 500 millilitre crystalloid boluses to a maximum of 4 litres before considering additional agents
Commence intravenous adrenaline infusion titrated to blood pressure and heart rate, and give intravenous glucagon 1 to 2 milligrams for beta-blocker mediated adrenaline resistance
Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 milligrams and intravenous chlorphenamine 10 milligrams as the primary treatment while the current adrenaline effect is assessed
Intravenous noradrenaline 10 micrograms per minute infusion as first-line vasopressor for refractory anaphylaxis with continued crystalloid at 250 millilitres per hour
Nebulised adrenaline 5 millilitres of 1:1000 with hydrocortisone 200 milligrams IV and salbutamol 5 milligrams nebuliser as combined therapy for airway symptoms

subtopic_detail: Tumour lysis syndrome prophylaxis choice
stem:
A 42-year-old man newly diagnosed with Burkitt lymphoma is admitted to your haematology ward for CODOX-M induction chemotherapy. He has bulky abdominal disease, a serum lactate dehydrogenase over four times the upper limit of normal, and a white cell count of 68 x10^9/L. He is of African heritage and has no known glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; his G6PD screen has just returned as normal.

His serum uric acid is 0.55 mmol/L, corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L, phosphate 1.6 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, and creatinine 108 micromol/L. He has received 3 litres of intravenous Hartmann's solution over the last 12 hours and his urine output has been 100 mL per hour. Chemotherapy is planned to start within the next 12 hours. He weighs 72 kilograms.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 118/72, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, temp 37.2 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; palpable bulky abdominal lymphadenopathy; hepatosplenomegaly with liver 6 cm below costal margin; no rash; no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Uric acid 0.55 mmol/L; corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L; phosphate 1.6 mmol/L; potassium 4.8 mmol/L; creatinine 108 micromol/L; LDH 1620 U/L; white cell count 68 x10^9/L; G6PD screen normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate tumour lysis syndrome prophylaxis?

options.text: Oral allopurinol 300 milligrams daily and continue intravenous crystalloid at 3 litres per square metre per day with 4 hourly biochemistry monitoring for the first 24 hours
Prophylactic haemodialysis prior to induction chemotherapy with a target urea reduction ratio of 65 percent before the first dose of chemotherapy
Oral febuxostat 80 milligrams daily and sodium bicarbonate infusion to urinary pH above 7.5 with intravenous crystalloid at 4 litres per square metre daily
Intravenous rasburicase 0.2 milligrams per kilogram single dose and continue intravenous crystalloid at 3 litres per square metre per day with 4 hourly biochemistry monitoring
Delay induction chemotherapy for 48 hours and commence oral allopurinol 300 milligrams three times daily with sodium bicarbonate infusion for urinary alkalinisation

subtopic_detail: STEMI reperfusion PCI versus fibrinolysis
stem: A 55-year-old man presents to your regional emergency department with 90 minutes of central crushing chest pain. His ECG shows 3 mm ST elevation in the anterior leads with reciprocal changes. The nearest PCI-capable hospital is 3 hours away by road transport. Air retrieval is not available for at least 2 hours. Troponin has been sent. He has no contraindications to thrombolysis. He weighs 82 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 132/82, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Alert, in pain, no basal crackles, JVP not elevated, no pulmonary oedema, no new murmurs
data_table.Investigations: ECG: 3 mm ST elevation V1 to V4, reciprocal depression II, III, aVF; troponin pending; potassium 4.1; creatinine 90; INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Immediate transfer to the PCI centre for primary PCI, targeting a door-to-balloon time of 90 minutes from arrival at the receiving centre for optimal reperfusion outcomes
Wait for the troponin result then start dual antiplatelet therapy and heparin, and admit for medical management without acute reperfusion until further test results are available
Intravenous streptokinase 1.5 million units over 60 minutes plus oral aspirin, then defer transfer until pain resolves and further reperfusion needs are reassessed by the retrieval team
Weight-adjusted IV tenecteplase (about 40 mg) plus enoxaparin and clopidogrel now, then transfer for rescue PCI if reperfusion fails or routine early angiography 3 to 24 hours

IV glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to pain relief, oral aspirin and metoprolol, and admit locally for medical management until pain resolves and the troponin trajectory becomes clearer over time

subtopic_detail: Community-acquired pneumonia moderate severity
stem: A 65-year-old man presents to your emergency department with 3 days of productive cough, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and fever. He has a background of well-controlled type 2 diabetes. On examination he has right lower zone crackles and bronchial breathing. Chest x-ray shows a dense right lower lobe consolidation. Confusion Assessment Method is negative. His CURB-65 score is 1 (age 65 or over, plus one additional point).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 128/78, RR 26, SpO2 91 percent room air, temp 38.6 C
data_table.Examination: Alert, orientated, right lower zone crackles and bronchial breathing, no signs of shock
data_table.Investigations: Urea 6.2 mmol/L, WCC 18, CRP 240, sodium 138, creatinine 90; CXR right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic strategy?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 5 days, home management with a general practitioner review at 48 hours to reassess
IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours plus IV azithromycin 500 mg once daily for 7 days total, targeting broad spectrum cover for the community-acquired pneumonia observed today
IV ceftriaxone 2 g once daily plus IV vancomycin 15 mg/kg twice daily for 10 days, providing empirical MRSA cover for the community-acquired pneumonia observed today at admission
Oral moxifloxacin 400 mg once daily for 5 days plus oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days, then discharge home to community with a general practitioner follow-up appointment in 2 days
IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days total, then switch to oral therapy once he is clinically stable and improving

subtopic_detail: Warfarin peri-procedural bridging for elective surgery
stem: A 68-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc score 4) is on warfarin with INR 2.5. She is scheduled for an elective knee arthroplasty in 7 days. She has no history of prior stroke or systemic embolism, no mechanical heart valve, and no recent (under 3 months) venous thromboembolism. She has moderate renal impairment with eGFR 45. There has been no recent bleeding.

data_table.Examination: Alert, well, ECG atrial fibrillation, no signs of embolism or bleeding
data_table.Investigations: INR 2.5, Hb 128, platelets 260, creatinine 105, eGFR 45

lead_in: What is the most appropriate peri-procedural anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery, no bridging heparin required, then restart warfarin 12 to 24 hours after surgery when adequate haemostasis has been achieved by the surgical team
Continue warfarin at usual dose throughout the perioperative period since the bleeding risk of primary knee arthroplasty is generally acceptably low in most patients undergoing the procedure
Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery and bridge with therapeutic-dose enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily starting 3 days before the operation and continuing until the day of surgery this year
Stop warfarin 3 days before surgery and give oral vitamin K 5 mg to accelerate INR normalisation before the procedure and cross-match blood for the operation planned to occur this week
Switch warfarin to apixaban 5 mg twice daily starting 5 days before surgery, then hold apixaban 24 hours before the surgery scheduled for later next week and restart afterwards on advice

subtopic_detail: Hyponatraemia SIADH versus hypovolaemic differentiation
stem: A 74-year-old woman with newly diagnosed small cell lung cancer presents to your medical assessment unit with 5 days of nausea, unsteadiness and mild headache. She is on no diuretics. Her serum sodium is 118 mmol/L (baseline 138 two weeks ago), plasma osmolality 254 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 55 mmol/L. She is euvolaemic clinically. TSH and cortisol are normal. She is alert with no focal neurology.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 128/78 lying, 124/76 standing, RR 16, SpO2 97 percent, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Alert, orientated, no ataxia, no focal neurology, mucous membranes moist, JVP visible at 4 cm, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Na 118, K 4.0, urea 3.4, creatinine 60, plasma osm 254, urine osm 480, urine Na 55, TSH 1.8, cortisol 480

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Infuse 1 litre of 0.9 percent normal saline over 4 hours and reassess her sodium level after each litre until the serum sodium level reaches 130 mmol/L or above
Restrict fluids to 800 mL/day with sodium and neurological monitoring twice daily, aiming to raise serum sodium by no more than 8 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination
Give 3 percent hypertonic saline 150 mL bolus over 20 minutes to rapidly correct the serum sodium above 125 mmol/L within the next 4 hours, aiming to abolish symptoms quickly today
Prescribe oral demeclocycline 300 mg four times daily and continue an unrestricted oral fluid intake for maintenance, with monitoring of the serum sodium level daily on the ward round
Give IV furosemide 40 mg with oral salt tablets, then correct the serum sodium with a 2 percent saline infusion titrated overnight to rise no more than 8 mmol/L in the first 24 hours

subtopic_detail: HHS versus DKA insulin infusion approach
stem: A 76-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin and gliclazide presents to your emergency department after 5 days of polyuria and progressive drowsiness following a chest infection. His glucose is 42 mmol/L, sodium 152, potassium 4.0, urea 18, creatinine 130. Venous gas pH 7.34, bicarbonate 20, blood ketones 0.4 mmol/L. Calculated effective osmolality is 336 mOsm/kg. He is drowsy but rousable, significantly dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 100/60, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent, temp 37.6 C, weight 80 kg
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, GCS 13, dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, capillary refill 3 seconds, no focal neurology, chest crepitations right base
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 42, Na 152, K 4.0, urea 18, creatinine 130, VBG pH 7.34, HCO3 20, ketones 0.4, effective osm 336

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid and insulin approach?

options.text: IV 0.9 percent saline 1 litre over 1 hour, then continue at 250 mL/hour and commence IV insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour immediately once serum potassium is above 3.5 mmol/L
IV 0.9 percent saline 2 litres over 1 hour, commence IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately upon admission and aim for a glucose fall of 10 mmol/L per hour with observation
IV 0.9 percent saline 1 litre over 1 hour, reassess volume status, then only add low-dose insulin at 0.05 units/kg/hour if glucose fails to fall by 5 mmol/L per hour with fluids alone
IV 5 percent dextrose 1 litre over 2 hours, then an IV insulin bolus of 10 units followed by a 0.1 units/kg/hour infusion, targeting a glucose of 8 mmol/L within the next 4 hours today
IV Hartmann's 500 mL over 1 hour, commence subcutaneous insulin glargine 20 units at bedtime, treat chest infection and reassess him again in the morning on the ward round after handover

subtopic_detail: Contrast-induced nephropathy prevention
stem: A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and stage 3B chronic kidney disease (eGFR 38) is booked for a CT coronary angiogram tomorrow. His usual medications are metformin, ramipril, spironolactone, atorvastatin and gliclazide. He has recently increased his furosemide because of ankle swelling. His serum creatinine has been stable and his blood pressure is well controlled. He has no history of allergy to contrast media.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 74, BP 132/80, RR 16, weight 84 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert, mild pitting ankle oedema, chest clear, JVP not raised
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 155, eGFR 38, K 4.4, Hb 128, HbA1c 7.2 percent, BNP 240

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contrast nephropathy prevention plan?

options.text: Give IV N-acetylcysteine 1200 mg twice daily for 24 hours pre-procedure and 24 hours post-procedure, and continue all of his usual medications through the procedure without dose changes
Continue metformin and diuretics but withhold ramipril for 48 hours before the procedure, and no IV hydration is required for a patient with an eGFR greater than 30 mL/min/1.73m2 undergoing contrast

Prescribe oral sodium bicarbonate 3 g twice daily for 3 days before and 3 days after the procedure without other measures for prevention of contrast-induced nephropathy in this high-risk patient today

Withhold metformin, spironolactone, ramipril and furosemide from the day of procedure, IV 0.9 percent saline at 1 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours before and 12 hours after, use lowest effective iso-osmolar contrast

Cancel the CT coronary angiogram and proceed to invasive coronary angiography with a stress cardiac MRI to avoid all contrast exposure for the patient in view of his renal impairment and comorbidities

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotics in urosepsis with recent ESBL history
stem: A 78-year-old woman is transferred from her nursing home to your emergency department with 24 hours of confusion, fever and hypotension. She is known to have recurrent urinary tract infections and has had two admissions for ESBL Escherichia coli urosepsis in the past 6 months. On examination she is drowsy, hypotensive despite 2 litres of IV fluids, and has suprapubic tenderness. Bloods show creatinine 220 (baseline 90), lactate 3.6 and CRP 320. She is not pregnant.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 88/54 (post 2 L fluids), RR 26, SpO2 96 percent, temp 39.1 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, GCS 13, warm peripheries, capillary refill 3 seconds, suprapubic tenderness, no flank pain
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 220 (baseline 90), urea 14, lactate 3.6, WCC 22, CRP 320, urinalysis leucocytes and nitrites positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic and dosing decision?

options.text: IV amoxicillin 2 g every 6 hours plus IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily until cultures return with sensitivities, with standard renal dose adjustment being applied for gentamicin in her acute kidney injury

IV ceftriaxone 2 g once daily as empirical monotherapy, then add ampicillin only if enterococcal cover is judged required by microbiology, and continue ward-based care with hourly BP monitoring overnight

IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours dose-reduced for the acute kidney injury, and continue ward-based care with hourly blood pressure monitoring and delayed reassessment in the morning ward round

IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading then 15 mg/kg every 12 hours, plus IV metronidazole 500 mg every 8 hours for anaerobic cover, and admit her under general medicine for ongoing care and daily specialist review
IV meropenem 1 g every 8 hours dose-adjusted for creatinine clearance, obtain blood and urine cultures before the first dose, and escalate to ICU for haemodynamic support and vasopressors

subtopic_detail: Latent TB workup and treatment
stem: A 34-year-old woman migrated from Vietnam 6 months ago and attends your general practice for routine health assessment. She is well with no cough, no fever, no weight loss and no night sweats. She has never been treated for tuberculosis but recalls a household contact with active TB when she was 15. She is HIV negative and not immunosuppressed. Chest X-ray is clear. Her QFT-Plus is positive. She wishes to have children within 12 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Systemically well; clear chest on auscultation; no lymphadenopathy; no skin findings
data_table.Investigations: QFT-Plus positive; chest X-ray no active disease; HIV negative; HBV/HCV negative; LFTs within normal limits; not pregnant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment offer?

options.text: Rifampicin 600 mg orally daily plus isoniazid 300 mg orally daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg orally daily for 3 months (3HR) with monthly LFT and hepatitis symptom review during treatment
Isoniazid 300 mg orally daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg orally daily for 9 months (9H) as this remains the AU first-line regimen for latent TB in adults with normal baseline liver function
Rifampicin 600 mg orally daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg orally daily monotherapy for 4 months (4R) with monthly LFT monitoring and screening for drug interactions including hormonal contraception
No treatment as latent TB is asymptomatic and treatment risk outweighs benefit in a low-transmission country like Australia, provide symptom checklist and annual review in general practice

Repeat QFT-Plus in 6 months to confirm the positive result before commencing any treatment, as isolated QFT-Plus positivity has a false positive rate that warrants a repeat test for diagnostic certainty

subtopic_detail: Cushing syndrome screening choice
stem: A 44-year-old woman presents to your general practice concerned about a 12 kg weight gain over 6 months despite unchanged diet. She has developed acne, easy bruising on her forearms and reports low mood. On examination she has central obesity, wide purple striae on her abdomen and a rounded plethoric face. Her BP is 158/94. She is not on exogenous steroids and works day shifts as an accountant with a regular sleep schedule. Fasting glucose is 8.1 mmol/L on today's finger-prick test.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 158/94, RR 14, SpO2 99 percent, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Central obesity, moon facies, dorsocervical fat pad, wide purple striae on abdomen; proximal muscle weakness on rising from chair without arms; supraclavicular fullness
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 8.1 mmol/L (<7.0), HbA1c 6.8 percent (<5.7); TSH 2.1 mIU/L; UEC and calcium within normal limits; not on exogenous glucocorticoids; not pregnant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial screening test?

options.text: Serum ACTH morning level with paired cortisol as the initial screening test, expecting an elevated ACTH to indicate pituitary Cushing and a suppressed ACTH to indicate adrenal Cushing directly
Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test with a morning serum cortisol at 8 am, considering a cortisol below 50 nmol/L as an adequate response and above 50 nmol/L as an abnormal screen
Single 8 am morning serum cortisol level, with a value above the upper limit of normal (over 550 nmol/L) considered diagnostic of Cushing syndrome and prompting immediate imaging referral
Serum aldosterone-to-renin ratio measured in the morning after 2 hours upright posture as the initial screen given the hypertension and hypokalaemia are commonly associated with primary aldosteronism

MRI pituitary with dynamic contrast enhancement as the initial investigation given the classical clinical picture is highly suggestive of pituitary adenoma causing Cushing disease in this scenario today

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis initial pharmacotherapy
stem: A 68-year-old post-menopausal woman is referred to your general practice for review after a low-trauma wrist fracture 4 weeks ago from a fall from standing height. She smokes 10 cigarettes daily, drinks 3 standard drinks daily and has been on prednisolone 7.5 mg orally daily for polymyalgia rheumatica for 8 months. Her DEXA scan shows lumbar spine T-score -2.8 and femoral neck T-score -2.5. Her mother had a hip fracture at age 74. Her calcium and vitamin D are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mildly kyphotic thoracic spine; no acute back tenderness; no visible dental disease; no active infection
data_table.Investigations: DEXA lumbar T -2.8, femoral neck T -2.5; calcium 2.36 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.55), 25-OH vitamin D 68 nmol/L (>=50), eGFR 76 mL/min/1.73 m2; PTH 3.8 pmol/L (1.6 to 7.2), TSH 2.1 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: IV zoledronic acid 5 mg once yearly infusion as first-line pharmacotherapy as she has ongoing steroid exposure, and no dental review or renal check is required as her eGFR is above 35 mL/min

Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneous every 6 months as first-line pharmacotherapy without any prior bisphosphonate trial and without long-term commitment to a follow-on antiresorptive after eventual cessation

Teriparatide 20 microgram subcutaneous daily for 18 months as first-line anabolic therapy given the very low T-scores and glucocorticoid use as the anabolic pathway is more effective than antiresorptive
Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly on an empty stomach with 200 mL water and remain upright for 30 minutes, calcium and vitamin D optimisation, dental review before starting, and 5-year review
Increase oral calcium to 1500 mg daily plus vitamin D 2000 IU daily and lifestyle modification alone for 12 months, review DEXA at 12 months before considering any specific antiresorptive therapy

subtopic_detail: Endocarditis Duke criteria and empiric therapy
stem: A 62-year-old man presents to your emergency department with 2 weeks of intermittent fevers, night sweats and 4 kg weight loss. He had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement 3 months ago. On examination he has a new soft early diastolic murmur, splinter haemorrhages under two fingernails and tender nodules on the pulp of his index finger. Three sets of blood cultures drawn 1 hour apart are all positive for Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis). Transthoracic echo shows a mobile 1.2 cm echogenic mass on the aortic prosthesis with mild aortic regurgitation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 132/62, RR 18, SpO2 96 percent, temp 38.4 C
data_table.Examination: Splinter haemorrhages under two fingernails; tender pulp nodules on index finger (Osler nodes); new soft early diastolic aortic murmur; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Blood cultures x3 all positive S. gallolyticus; TTE 1.2 cm mobile aortic prosthesis vegetation; mild AR; CRP 92 mg/L (<5); WCC 15 x10^9/L; creatinine 92 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management combination?

options.text: IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading then 15 mg/kg every 12 hours monotherapy for 6 weeks and defer any surgical review or transoesophageal echo pending clinical improvement over the next 5 to 7 days
IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily monotherapy for 4 weeks and observation without cardiothoracic surgical consultation as vegetations under 2 cm rarely embolise and the mild aortic regurgitation is stable

IV benzylpenicillin 2.4 g every 4 hours plus IV gentamicin 3 mg/kg daily for 6 weeks total, arrange transoesophageal echo, colonoscopy for occult colorectal malignancy and cardiothoracic surgery review

IV flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours plus IV rifampicin 600 mg orally twice daily for suspected staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis empirically before waiting for the confirmed culture identification

Broad-spectrum empirical piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours pending susceptibility results, with home IV therapy commenced through the outpatient antimicrobial program once afebrile for 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis recognition and management
stem: A 43-year-old woman with a background of Hashimoto thyroiditis on levothyroxine presents to your emergency department with 2 days of vomiting, abdominal pain and profound fatigue. She has felt increasingly weak, dizzy on standing and salt-craving over 3 months. She is otherwise on no medications. On examination she has hyperpigmentation of her palmar creases, buccal mucosa and recent surgical scar from an appendicectomy 10 years ago. Blood pressure is 78/48 mmHg. She is severely dehydrated and has never taken glucocorticoids.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 78/48, RR 22, SpO2 98 percent, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Hyperpigmented palmar creases, buccal mucosa, old surgical scar; dry mucous membranes; supine BP drops from 92 to 78/48 on sitting; peripherally cool; no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L (135 to 145), K 5.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L, TSH 4.8 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), VBG pH 7.32; morning cortisol pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV dexamethasone 4 mg stat before drawing morning cortisol and ACTH samples, IV Hartmann 1000 mL over the first hour and observe supine BP before further pharmacological intervention
Increase levothyroxine to 200 microgram orally daily for suspected myxoedema coma, IV normal saline 500 mL over 30 minutes and cover with ceftriaxone 2 g pending source review of infection today

IV insulin actrapid 5 unit and 50 mL 50 percent dextrose for hyperkalaemia, IV calcium gluconate 10 mL 10 percent for cardioprotection and IV furosemide 40 mg for potassium excretion while awaiting cortisol

Observation with strict input output monitoring and repeat serum cortisol at 8 am the following day before commencing any glucocorticoid replacement to avoid confounding the diagnostic biochemistry today
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 200 mg over 24 hours infusion, IV normal saline 1000 mL over first hour, IV 10 percent dextrose 500 mL for hypoglycaemia and hold the levothyroxine dose today

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis recognition
stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to your emergency department with 24 hours of severe left leg pain out of proportion to the visible skin appearance. He fell in the garden 3 days ago with a small abrasion to his left shin. Today the leg is swollen with a small area of erythema over the shin. His HR is 128, BP 96/60, temperature 39.2 C. He is confused and cold peripherally. On palpation there is crepitus over the calf and pain extending well beyond the visible erythema.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 96/60, RR 26, SpO2 96 percent, temp 39.2 C, cap refill 4 seconds, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Small erythematous patch over shin with a 5 mm scab; pain and swelling extending well beyond visible erythema; crepitus on palpation of calf; foot cool with intact pulses; no bullae yet
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L (4 to 11), CRP 285 mg/L (<5), Na 128 mmol/L (135 to 145), creatinine 168 micromol/L (<110), glucose 15.6 mmol/L, Hb 118 g/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L (<2), CK 890 U/L (<200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Urgent surgical consultation for wide debridement in theatre within 1 hour, IV meropenem 1 g and IV clindamycin 900 mg empirically, IV fluid resuscitation and blood cultures without delaying surgery

IV flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours for standard cellulitis, IV normal saline 500 mL bolus, elevate the leg and mark the erythema border for reassessment in 4 hours before deciding on any further imaging

CT lower limb with IV contrast to confirm gas in tissue planes before surgical consultation, with commencement of vancomycin and cefepime broad-spectrum antibiotics once radiological confirmation is obtained
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy referral as adjunctive treatment before surgical debridement is performed, with IV benzylpenicillin monotherapy for suspected clostridial gas gangrene from the garden wound

IV ceftriaxone 2 g monotherapy with tetanus booster and topical mupirocin to the abrasion, planned admission to the medical ward for observation and outpatient surgical review within 48 hours if the pain persists

subtopic_detail: Type A aortic dissection recognition and initial management
stem: A 64-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension presents to your emergency department with 45 minutes of sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to his back. He is diaphoretic and looks unwell. On examination his right arm BP is 178/98 and left arm BP is 128/72. He has a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. ECG shows sinus rhythm with 1 mm ST depression in V4 to V6 without ST elevation. Bedside troponin is mildly elevated at 42 ng/L (<14).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 178/98 right arm and 128/72 left arm, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, alert; soft early diastolic murmur at LSE; right radial pulse full, left radial reduced volume; symmetrical lower limb pulses; no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm, 1 mm ST depression V4 to V6, no STE; troponin 42 ng/L (<14); chest X-ray widened mediastinum >8 cm; VBG pH 7.34, lactate 2.4 mmol/L (<2); creatinine 108 micromol/L (<110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV sodium nitroprusside infusion titrated to systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg first, then IV metoprolol 5 mg boluses for rate control, plus IV aspirin 300 mg and heparin 5000 units for acute coronary syndrome
