IV labetalol infusion titrated to HR 60 and systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg first before any vasodilator, urgent CT aortogram, cardiothoracic surgical activation, and hold antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for now
Immediate cardiac catheterisation for suspected NSTEMI given the ST depression, elevated troponin and chest pain, deferring aortic imaging until angiography excludes an acute coronary syndrome first

IV hydralazine 20 mg bolus every 20 minutes for BP control, oral aspirin 300 mg loading, oral clopidogrel 300 mg loading and admit to the coronary care unit for continuous cardiac monitoring overnight

Thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg IV over 90 minutes for suspected STEMI equivalent posterior wall infarction given the persistent ST depression V4 to V6 in this high risk chest pain presentation today

subtopic_detail: Community-acquired pneumonia
stem: You are the medical registrar in an Australian metropolitan emergency department reviewing a 62-year-old man with 4 days of productive cough, right-sided pleuritic chest pain, fever and progressive breathlessness. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. His medications are metformin, perindopril and atorvastatin. He is not immunocompromised. He lives independently and has had no recent hospital admissions or overseas travel. He is up to date with pneumococcal and influenza vaccination. On examination he has bronchial breathing in the right mid-zone and dullness to percussion. Chest radiograph shows dense right middle-lobe consolidation without effusion.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 108/64, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 91% on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: white cells 15.6 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), CRP 168 mg/L (<5), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), urea 9.1 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), lactate 2.4 mmol/L (<2), albumin 34 g/L (35-50), venous pH 7.36 (7.35-7.45), chest radiograph right middle-lobe consolidation without effusion
data_table.History: T2DM, hypertension, up to date pneumococcal and influenza, lives independently, no recent hospitalisation, no travel, no immunosuppression

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen and disposition?

options.text: Discharge home on oral amoxicillin 1 g every 8 hours for 5 days with general practitioner review at 48 hours
Admit to ward on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily as monotherapy
Admit to intensive care on intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam plus intravenous vancomycin loading dose
Admit to ward on oral clarithromycin 500 mg every 12 hours as macrolide monotherapy for 5 days total
Admit to ward on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily

subtopic_detail: Provoked DVT anticoagulation duration
stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 54-year-old man 3 months after diagnosis of a right proximal femoral vein deep vein thrombosis. The DVT occurred 4 weeks after right total knee replacement with a 6-week postoperative period of significantly reduced mobility. He has no family history of thrombosis, no prior VTE, no active malignancy, no antiphospholipid syndrome, and no ongoing prothrombotic risk factors. He has completed 3 months of apixaban 5 mg twice daily without bleeding, has walked without ongoing swelling for the past 6 weeks, and has returned to normal daily activity. He asks how long he needs to remain on anticoagulation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 72, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 138 g/L (135-170), platelets 240 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m2, LFTs within normal limits, D-dimer not indicated at this time
data_table.History: 3 months of apixaban 5 mg BD after post-arthroplasty proximal DVT, no ongoing bleeding, no residual swelling for 6 weeks, no personal or family thrombotic history, no cancer or APS

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan from today?

options.text: Stop apixaban now and provide written advice on venous thromboembolism prevention for future surgery
Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely as extended anticoagulation for the proximal deep vein thrombosis
Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily and continue indefinitely as extended prophylactic anticoagulation
Switch to aspirin 100 mg daily indefinitely as extended venous thromboembolism recurrence prevention
Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily for a further 3 months then stop and provide written VTE advice

subtopic_detail: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes
stem: You are the emergency department registrar. A 71-year-old man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline creatinine 260 micromol/L, eGFR 20 mL/min/1.73 m2) is brought in by paramedics for progressive weakness over 2 days. He takes perindopril, spironolactone and slow-K supplementation for prior hypokalaemia (last review 6 months ago). ECG on arrival shows peaked T waves in V2 to V5 and a prolonged PR interval of 240 ms. He is awake, chest is clear, no ischaemic chest pain, blood pressure and heart rate are stable. Point-of-care venous gas gives potassium 7.4 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 68, blood pressure 138/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: potassium 7.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0) on VBG, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22-32), creatinine 340 micromol/L (60-110) vs baseline 260, glucose 6.8 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), pH 7.28 (7.35-7.45), ECG peaked T waves V2-V5 and PR 240 ms
data_table.History: CKD stage 4 baseline creatinine 260, medications perindopril, spironolactone, slow-K, no chest pain, no diabetes-related hypoglycaemia risk

lead_in: Which intervention should you perform FIRST?

options.text: Give intravenous insulin 10 units in 50 mL of 50% glucose over 20 minutes as the initial hyperkalaemia therapy
Give intravenous calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 2 to 5 minutes with continuous cardiac rhythm monitoring
Give nebulised salbutamol 10 mg over 10 minutes as the initial intracellular potassium-shift therapy
Give oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g with sorbitol as the initial potassium-removal therapy
Call renal services for urgent haemodialysis today and defer any other therapy until dialysis can start

subtopic_detail: Sepsis hour-1 bundle and vasopressor initiation
stem: You are the medical registrar in an Australian emergency department. A 68-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and moderate CKD (baseline creatinine 130 micromol/L) is brought in with rigors, dysuria, right-flank pain and confusion. She is quickly recognised as having urosepsis. Within 30 minutes she has received IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg and IV amoxicillin-clavulanate. She has received 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid over 90 minutes. Her repeat lactate 60 minutes after starting fluids has risen from 4.2 to 5.1 mmol/L. She remains hypotensive with mean arterial pressure of 58 mmHg despite the completed bolus. Blood cultures were drawn before antibiotics.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 82/44 (MAP 58), respiratory rate 26, SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal prongs, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: white cells 22.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), CRP 316 mg/L (<5), lactate 5.1 mmol/L (was 4.2), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 240 micromol/L (baseline 130), venous pH 7.28 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 16 mmol/L, urinalysis heavy nitrites and blood
data_table.History: T2DM, CKD baseline creatinine 130, urosepsis on antibiotics for 45 minutes, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid completed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a further 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus over 60 minutes and reassess lactate and blood pressure in one hour
Commence peripheral noradrenaline infusion via a large-bore antecubital vein while central access is being established
Give intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg loading dose before starting vasopressor therapy for septic shock
Escalate to intravenous meropenem 1 g plus vancomycin loading dose 25 mg/kg for likely resistant urosepsis coverage
Delay commencing vasopressor therapy until the mean arterial pressure falls below 55 mmHg despite ongoing fluids

subtopic_detail: First demyelinating event and McDonald criteria
stem: You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner. Over the last 10 days she has developed progressive vision loss in her right eye with pain on eye movement. Ten months ago she had a 3-week episode of numbness across the right hemibody that resolved fully and she attributed it to stress and did not seek medical review at the time. She has no other medical history and takes no medications. On examination today her right visual acuity is 6/24 with a right relative afferent pupillary defect and a subtle red desaturation on the right; left eye 6/6. Neurological examination is otherwise normal. Fundoscopy shows a mildly swollen right optic disc.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 76, blood pressure 122/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, TSH within normal limits, HIV and syphilis serology negative, ANA negative, vitamin B12 380 pmol/L (>200), MRI brain and spine shows one enhancing right optic nerve lesion plus 4 non-enhancing periventricular T2 lesions plus 1 spinal cord T2 lesion at C4 plus 1 juxtacortical T2 lesion, no infratentorial lesion, CSF oligoclonal bands positive (not present in serum), aquaporin-4 antibody negative, MOG-IgG negative
data_table.History: 10 months ago transient right hemibody numbness for 3 weeks, now right optic neuritis, no other medical history, no medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic conclusion and next step?

options.text: Clinically isolated syndrome with insufficient evidence for a multiple sclerosis diagnosis; repeat magnetic resonance imaging in 3 months
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder based on optic and spinal cord involvement; commence rituximab this admission
Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis meeting 2017 McDonald criteria; give IV methylprednisolone and refer for DMT
Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein-antibody-associated disease; commence high-dose oral prednisone taper only today
Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis; refer for ovarian teratoma workup and plasmapheresis this admission

subtopic_detail: Haemodynamically unstable pulmonary embolism
stem: You are the medical registrar in the emergency department resuscitation cubicle. A 62-year-old man presented 20 minutes ago with sudden onset dyspnoea and syncope 40 minutes after arriving from an interstate flight. He is now clammy, breathless and confused. Point-of-care ultrasound shows a dilated right ventricle with poor contractility. Bedside troponin is 380 ng/L (upper reference 30) and NT-proBNP is 3400 pg/mL. He weighs 92 kg. His IV access is patent. He has no active bleeding, no recent surgery, no stroke, no known intracranial pathology, no bleeding disorder, no anticoagulation, no allergy. His wife confirms no head injury and no gastrointestinal bleeding in the last month.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 76/42, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 88% on 15 L non-rebreather, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: troponin 380 ng/L (<30), NT-proBNP 3400 pg/mL (<450), lactate 3.8 mmol/L (<2), venous pH 7.30 (7.35-7.45), full blood count within normal limits, INR 1.1, creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), point-of-care ultrasound dilated hypokinetic right ventricle with septal flattening; CT pulmonary angiogram unavailable in the next 10 minutes
data_table.History: Long-haul flight, sudden dyspnoea and syncope, no bleeding, no surgery, no stroke, no intracranial pathology, no anticoagulation, no allergy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence unfractionated heparin infusion at 80 units per kilogram bolus and await computed tomography pulmonary angiography
Commence intravenous adrenaline infusion, intubate for airway control, and defer thrombolysis until CT head done
Give an intravenous 20 mL/kg fluid bolus and add dobutamine infusion for right ventricular support without thrombolysis
Administer systemic alteplase 100 mg intravenously over 2 hours with concurrent unfractionated heparin per protocol
Refer for emergency surgical pulmonary embolectomy without giving any medical thrombolysis first this admission

subtopic_detail: Cardiogenic shock post-STEMI mechanical circulatory support
stem: You are the cardiology registrar in the coronary care unit. A 64-year-old man had a large anterior STEMI 6 hours ago treated with primary PCI to the proximal LAD with successful stent deployment and TIMI 3 flow. Since return from the catheter laboratory he has developed cardiogenic shock: MAP 55 mmHg despite noradrenaline at 0.4 microgram/kg/min plus adrenaline at 0.15 microgram/kg/min, lactate 5.8 mmol/L rising from 4.4, urine output 5 mL/h, and mottled peripheries. Bedside echocardiogram shows LV EF 20% with global anterior akinesis, no mechanical complication (no VSD, no papillary muscle rupture, no free wall rupture), no pericardial effusion. Right ventricular function is preserved. Coronary anatomy confirms complete revascularisation. He has been intubated 30 minutes ago and remains on high FiO2.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 112 (sinus tachycardia), blood pressure 92/38 with MAP 55, respiratory rate 22 (ventilated), SpO2 92% on FiO2 0.8, temperature 36.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: troponin 25000 ng/L (<30), lactate 5.8 mmol/L rising from 4.4 (<2), creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110) rising from 90, mixed venous saturation 45%, echocardiogram LV EF 20%, global anterior akinesis, no mechanical complication, RV preserved, no effusion; ECG anterior Q waves with residual ST elevation
data_table.History: Anterior STEMI 6 hours ago, primary PCI proximal LAD with TIMI 3 flow, complete revascularisation, intubated 30 min ago

lead_in: According to the most contemporary Australian and international evidence, what is the most appropriate mechanical circulatory support decision?

options.text: Insert an intra-aortic balloon pump now and continue the current noradrenaline plus adrenaline vasoactive support
Increase noradrenaline to 0.6 microgram/kg/min and add a vasopressin infusion at 0.03 units per minute together
Commence a dobutamine infusion at 5 microgram/kg/min in addition to the current noradrenaline and adrenaline
Initiate emergency haemodialysis today for lactate clearance and continue current vasoactive support otherwise
Initiate veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation as bridge to recovery with concurrent LV venting strategy

subtopic_detail: Atrial fibrillation stroke prevention
stem: You are the GP seeing a 68-year-old woman with new persistent atrial fibrillation confirmed on 12-lead ECG and Holter. She has hypertension (on perindopril), type 2 diabetes (on metformin, HbA1c 7.0 percent), and no history of stroke, heart failure, vascular disease, or bleeding. Her BP today is 132/82, weight 78 kg, and creatinine 82 umol/L (eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m^2). She has no significant valvular heart disease on echo. She is symptomatic with palpitations but rate is controlled at 88 bpm on bisoprolol.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88 irregular, blood pressure 132/82, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.History: New persistent AF, HTN, T2DM, no stroke/HF/vascular disease, no bleeding history
data_table.Bloods: creatinine 82 umol/L (45-90), eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m^2, HbA1c 7.0 percent, weight 78 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate stroke prevention strategy?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally daily as antithrombotic therapy for atrial fibrillation with the score less than four total
Start apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily long-term unless a specific contraindication develops during ongoing review
No antithrombotic therapy since the annual stroke risk is low enough to permit conservative management strategy
Warfarin targeting INR 2.5 with weekly monitoring by community pathology and pharmacist-led dose adjustment
Dual antiplatelet clopidogrel plus aspirin as an alternative to anticoagulation in patients with adequate rate control

subtopic_detail: Acute ischaemic stroke thrombolysis
stem: You are the ED registrar seeing a 68-year-old man brought in 2 hours after sudden right-sided weakness and dysphasia witnessed by his wife. NIHSS is 12 (right hemiparesis, expressive aphasia, gaze preference). He has hypertension (on ramipril) and is on aspirin 100 mg daily. He has no recent surgery, no head injury, no bleeding, no anticoagulation, and no seizure with onset. His INR is 1.0. BP is currently 168/94. CT brain shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct; CTA shows a proximal M1 occlusion on the left MCA.

data_table.Vital signs: blood pressure 168/94, pulse 82 regular, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Investigations: CT brain no haemorrhage or established infarct; CTA left M1 occlusion; BSL 6.8 mmol/L; INR 1.0; platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give aspirin 300 mg orally now, admit to stroke unit, arrange elective thrombectomy tomorrow morning after MRI
Give IV labetalol 20 mg to lower blood pressure to below 140/80 before considering any reperfusion therapy option
Give IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (10 percent bolus, remainder over 60 min) plus arrange endovascular thrombectomy now
Give IV heparin infusion to prevent clot propagation and reassess in 24 hours for further reperfusion candidacy
Withhold thrombolysis due to prior aspirin use and instead administer IV nimodipine and admit for expectant care

subtopic_detail: Acute severe asthma exacerbation
stem: You are the ED registrar seeing a 26-year-old woman with a known history of asthma presenting with 6 hours of worsening breathlessness. She can speak in short phrases only. She has been using her salbutamol MDI hourly with minimal improvement. She has no fever, no chest pain, no haemoptysis, and no recent COVID or influenza-like illness. She has never been intubated for asthma. She takes budesonide/formoterol 200/6 mcg twice daily but admits variable adherence. She has no allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, respiratory rate 30, blood pressure 122/76, SpO2 90% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Widespread wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase, accessory muscle use, no cyanosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Non-invasive ventilation with BiPAP settings 12/6 as first-line management before any bronchodilator escalation attempted
Oral amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 5 days plus a salbutamol MDI with spacer 4 puffs 4-hourly and outpatient GP follow-up
IV theophylline 250 mg loading dose over 20 min as first-line bronchodilator before nebulised salbutamol trial
Salbutamol 5 mg plus ipratropium 500 mcg nebulised, oxygen to target 93 to 95 percent, and oral prednisolone 50 mg
Adrenaline 0.5 mg IM to lateral thigh as initial bronchodilator therapy before nebulised beta-agonist administration

subtopic_detail: Type 2 diabetes second-line pharmacotherapy
stem: You are the GP seeing a 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 8 years, on metformin 1 g twice daily, with an HbA1c of 8.4 percent (target <7 percent). He has hypertension (on perindopril), stable ischaemic heart disease with prior MI 3 years ago (on aspirin, atorvastatin, bisoprolol), and eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m^2. His weight is 94 kg (BMI 31), BP 128/78, and there is no diabetic ketoacidosis, no recurrent UTI or genital infection, and no history of DKA-precipitating illness. He has good renal function and no diabetic foot ulcers.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 72, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, weight 94 kg
data_table.Bloods: HbA1c 8.4 percent, eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m^2, creatinine 92 umol/L (60-110), LDL 1.8 mmol/L on statin
data_table.Comorbidity: Prior MI 3 years ago, HTN, no DKA history, no recurrent GU infections, no foot ulcers

lead_in: What is the most appropriate add-on to metformin?

options.text: Add gliclazide MR 60 mg oral daily titrated up over 6 weeks and continue metformin for glycaemic control only
Add basal insulin glargine 10 units subcutaneously nocte titrated by 2 units every 3 days for glycaemic control
Add pioglitazone 30 mg oral daily to improve insulin sensitivity and continue metformin for durable glycaemic control
Add sitagliptin 100 mg oral daily as weight-neutral therapy with low hypoglycaemia risk and continue metformin fully
Add empagliflozin 10 mg oral daily and continue metformin for combined cardiovascular and glycaemic benefit

subtopic_detail: Pheochromocytoma pre-operative preparation
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 44-year-old woman referred for episodic hypertension with headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis lasting 15 to 20 minutes several times weekly. Her home blood pressures range 148/92 to 210/126. She has lost 5 kg unintentionally over 3 months.

Investigations show plasma metanephrines: normetanephrine 4.8 nmol/L (below 0.9), metanephrine 3.1 nmol/L (below 0.5). 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines are also elevated at 4 times the upper limit. CT abdomen shows a 4.2 cm right adrenal mass with unenhanced attenuation of 32 Hounsfield units and heterogenous enhancement. The endocrine surgeon is planning laparoscopic adrenalectomy in 3 weeks. Her ECG shows normal sinus rhythm at 96 bpm with LVH by voltage criteria.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 178/108, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: plasma normetanephrine 4.8 nmol/L (<0.9), metanephrine 3.1 nmol/L (<0.5), potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 68 umol/L
data_table.Imaging: right adrenal mass 4.2 cm, 32 HU unenhanced, heterogenous enhancement, no metastases

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in preoperative preparation?

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion and admit for continuous BP monitoring until surgery is performed
Commence metoprolol 50 mg twice daily immediately to control heart rate and blood pressure ahead of surgery
Commence ramipril 10 mg daily and amlodipine 5 mg daily for blood pressure control before surgery
Proceed to laparoscopic adrenalectomy urgently without prior medical blockade to avoid drug side effects
Commence phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BD for at least 10 to 14 days, adding metoprolol closer to surgery only if tachycardia develops

subtopic_detail: Guillain-Barré syndrome ascending weakness with respiratory watch
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar admitting a 58-year-old man with 5 days of ascending symmetric weakness starting in his feet and now involving his thighs and hands. He had a diarrhoeal illness 3 weeks ago that self-resolved. On examination he has bilateral facial weakness. Power is 3/5 in lower limbs, 4/5 in upper limbs. Reflexes are absent throughout. Sensation shows mild distal glove-and-stocking paraesthesiae. His forced vital capacity at the bedside is 1.6 L (predicted 4.0 L). His maximum negative inspiratory force is minus 30 cmH2O. He has no bulbar symptoms today but coughed weakly.

CSF shows protein 1.2 g/L (below 0.45), cell count 3 x10^6/L (below 5), glucose normal. Nerve conduction studies are pending.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 138/86, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Neuro: power LL 3/5, UL 4/5, areflexic throughout, bilateral LMN facial weakness, mild sensory loss
data_table.Respiratory: FVC 1.6 L (40% predicted), NIF -30 cmH2O, weak cough

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Admit monitored, start IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days, and escalate to ICU if FVC falls below 1 litre or 20 mL/kg or NIF worsens
Commence oral prednisolone 60 mg daily and admit for observation until nerve conduction studies confirm the diagnosis
Discharge with outpatient neurology review because absence of bulbar symptoms and stable saturations reassure against near-term deterioration
Start plasma exchange and immediately follow with IVIG for combined effect, admitting to ICU regardless of respiratory parameters
Arrange urgent MRI whole spine to exclude cord compression before initiating any specific therapy for Guillain-Barré syndrome

subtopic_detail: Acute type A aortic dissection
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar assessing a 62-year-old man with sudden onset ripping interscapular chest pain radiating to the back and neck 90 minutes ago. He has hypertension on ramipril, poorly adherent. On examination his right arm blood pressure is 168/98, left arm 118/72 (differential 50 mmHg). There is a new early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Pulses in both radial arteries are palpable but unequal.

ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 108 with no acute ST changes. Chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum. CT aortogram is being reported now: the radiologist rings to tell you there is an intimal flap extending from the aortic root through the ascending aorta and into the aortic arch with false lumen involving the origin of the innominate artery. There is a small pericardial effusion but no tamponade physiology.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 168/98 right arm and 118/72 left arm, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Exam: diastolic murmur LSE, BP differential 50 mmHg, unequal radials
data_table.Imaging: widened mediastinum on CXR, CT aortogram intimal flap aortic root to arch, small pericardial effusion, no tamponade

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer aspirin 300 mg, ticagrelor 180 mg loading, and IV heparin, then transfer for urgent coronary angiography
Commence intravenous nitroprusside infusion to lower BP rapidly then arrange transfer for endovascular stent grafting
Commence IV esmolol targeting heart rate 60 and systolic BP 100 to 120, then immediately transfer to a cardiothoracic centre for repair
Admit to the cardiology ward for observation with oral beta blocker and analgesia, book non-urgent CT surveillance
Perform urgent pericardiocentesis in the ED before transfer to address the small pericardial effusion

subtopic_detail: Hypertensive emergency with acute pulmonary oedema
stem:
You are the ED registrar called for a 64-year-old woman with 2 hours of severe dyspnoea. She has a history of hypertension on ramipril, has stopped taking it for a fortnight because of a chest infection. On arrival she is speaking in single words, sitting upright, using accessory muscles. Blood pressure is 232/126, pulse 118, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 82 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 15 L/min via non-rebreather. Auscultation reveals bibasal crackles to mid-zones and an audible S3.

ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 118, LVH with strain. Chest X-ray shows bilateral perihilar interstitial oedema, no consolidation, no pneumothorax. Point-of-care troponin is mildly elevated at 42 ng/L (below 14). Bedside echocardiogram shows preserved LV ejection fraction of 60 percent, marked concentric hypertrophy, and B-lines throughout both lung fields.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 232/126, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 92% on 15 L/min NRB, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: troponin 42 ng/L (<14), creatinine 108 umol/L (45-90), potassium 4.1 mmol/L, BNP 812 pg/mL (<100)
data_table.Imaging: CXR bilateral interstitial oedema, echo LVEF 60% with concentric LVH, diffuse B-lines

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management combination?

options.text: Restart oral ramipril 10 mg immediately, give oral furosemide 40 mg, and reassess in an hour
Administer intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus and titrate to systolic BP below 140 mmHg within 30 minutes
Give intravenous morphine 5 mg and start heparin infusion for suspected coronary ischaemia given the troponin rise
Apply non-invasive positive pressure ventilation, start IV glyceryl trinitrate infusion, and give IV furosemide 40 mg
Intubate immediately and initiate mandatory mechanical ventilation before starting any vasoactive therapy

subtopic_detail: Adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis
stem:
You are the ED registrar assessing a 58-year-old man brought in by ambulance with 8 hours of severe headache, fever, and vomiting. His wife reports he became confused in the last hour. He has no known drug allergies, has a history of ischaemic heart disease, and is not immunocompromised. On examination he has a temperature of 39.4, GCS 13 (E3V4M6), photophobia, and neck stiffness. Kernig sign is positive. There is a small non-blanching petechial rash over his shins. He has no focal neurological deficit. There are no papilloedema on fundoscopy.

His observations are pulse 118, blood pressure 108/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96 percent on room air. Bedside glucose is 6.1 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 108/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Neuro: GCS 13 (E3V4M6), photophobia, neck stiffness, Kernig positive, no focal deficit, no papilloedema

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly first for suspected HSV encephalitis pending imaging and CSF results
Perform an urgent lumbar puncture immediately in ED for CSF analysis before giving antibiotics to preserve culture yield
Give IV ceftriaxone 2 g alone and defer benzylpenicillin because it adds no coverage beyond ceftriaxone in an adult
Withhold dexamethasone until CSF confirms pneumococcal meningitis to avoid immunosuppression during viral or aseptic causes
Take blood cultures, give IV dexamethasone 10 mg then IV ceftriaxone 2 g and benzylpenicillin 2.4 g together, then arrange CT and LP

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis in patient on chronic corticosteroids with intercurrent sepsis
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 54-year-old woman with 2 days of fever and productive cough. She has rheumatoid arthritis and has been on prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for 6 years, plus methotrexate. On arrival she is drowsy (GCS 13), pale, and diaphoretic. Blood pressure is 82/44, pulse 128, temperature 38.9, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 91 percent on room air. Chest exam reveals right basal crackles. Blood glucose is 3.2 mmol/L.

Bloods show sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, urea 12.4 mmol/L, creatinine 148 umol/L, CRP 220 mg/L, WCC 18.4 x10^9/L with left shift, lactate 4.2 mmol/L. Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. She has been given 500 mL Hartmann's, still hypotensive.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 82/44, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 91% on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 148 umol/L (45-90), glucose 3.2 mmol/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, CRP 220 mg/L (<5)
data_table.Chronic Rx: prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for 6 years, methotrexate 15 mg weekly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial priority alongside fluid resuscitation and antibiotics?

options.text: Double her usual oral prednisolone dose to 15 mg once she is able to swallow, and reassess in 6 hours
Administer hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus immediately, then 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion (or 50 mg IV 6-hourly)
Perform a short synacthen test now before giving any steroid to establish the diagnosis and guide long-term therapy
Give IV fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily to address the hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia
Withhold any additional corticosteroid pending blood cortisol result to avoid steroid-induced immunosuppression in sepsis

subtopic_detail: Suspected necrotising fasciitis lower limb
stem:
You are the surgical registrar called to ED for a 52-year-old man with 36 hours of a rapidly expanding painful red lower leg. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin. On arrival he is grey and diaphoretic. The affected leg has a poorly demarcated area of dusky discoloration extending from mid-shin to knee, with two 2 cm haemorrhagic bullae over the shin, and a small area of skin necrosis. He reports pain out of proportion to the visible signs. There is crepitus on palpation. He is confused.

Observations: pulse 132, blood pressure 92/54, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 39.2. Bloods show white cell count 21.6 x10^9/L, CRP 356 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, glucose 15.4 mmol/L, creatinine 168 umol/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L. LRINEC score is calculated at 9.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132, blood pressure 92/54, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: WCC 21.6 x10^9/L, CRP 356 mg/L (<5), sodium 132 mmol/L, glucose 15.4 mmol/L, creatinine 168 umol/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L
data_table.Exam: dusky lower leg, haemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, pain out of proportion, LRINEC 9

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Immediate surgical debridement in theatre with empiric IV meropenem, vancomycin, and clindamycin plus resuscitation en route
Arrange urgent MRI leg to confirm fascial involvement before proceeding with surgical debridement in theatre
Commence IV flucloxacillin 2 g 6-hourly for presumed cellulitis and observe for clinical response over 6 to 12 hours
Give IV vancomycin monotherapy, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, and defer any surgery until fully stabilised
Perform bedside skin biopsy for frozen section histology in the ED before theatre to confirm the diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Acute gout flare in a patient with chronic kidney disease
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 68-year-old man in the acute medical clinic with 24 hours of a very painful, red, swollen right first metatarsophalangeal joint. He has had two similar episodes previously that self-resolved with paracetamol over 5 to 7 days. He has stage 4 CKD with eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73 m2 (baseline 22 to 26), hypertension on amlodipine, ischaemic heart disease on aspirin, and takes no other regular medications. He is not on urate-lowering therapy.

On examination the right first MTP joint is warm, tender, erythematous with overlying skin taut and shiny, and range of motion is severely restricted by pain. There is a small tophaceous nodule on the right olecranon. He is afebrile, blood pressure 132/78, pulse 88. Serum urate today is 0.52 mmol/L (upper limit 0.42), creatinine 236 umol/L, CRP 68 mg/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: creatinine 236 umol/L (baseline 220-240), eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73 m2, urate 0.52 mmol/L (<0.42), CRP 68 mg/L (<5)
data_table.Exam: right first MTP joint warm, erythematous, swollen, tender, right olecranon tophus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line therapy for the acute flare?

options.text: Commence oral naproxen 500 mg BD for 5 days with a proton pump inhibitor for gastroprotection during acute treatment
Commence oral prednisolone 25 mg daily for 5 days and discuss commencing allopurinol at low dose after the acute flare has resolved
Commence oral colchicine 1 mg then 500 micrograms 1 hour later, then 500 micrograms 12-hourly for a full 3 days
Commence allopurinol 300 mg daily now to reduce serum urate and treat the acute flare simultaneously in one visit
Perform bedside joint aspiration for intra-articular corticosteroid injection and send synovial fluid for gram stain and crystals

subtopic_detail: Haemodynamic instability with echocardiographic RV strain
stem:
You are the medical registrar in ED reviewing a 58-year-old man with sudden dyspnoea and collapse 2 days after a long haul flight from Los Angeles. He has a heart rate of 132, blood pressure 82/48 despite 2 litres of crystalloid, and cool peripheries. Oxygen saturation is 88 percent on 15 litres via non-rebreather. Bedside echocardiogram shows a dilated hypokinetic right ventricle with paradoxical septal motion. CT pulmonary angiogram confirms bilateral saddle embolus. He is on no anticoagulant and has no bleeding contraindications.

The intensivist has intubation prepared and asks about definitive reperfusion.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132, blood pressure 82/48, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 88% on 15 L NRB, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 138 g/L (135-175), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 92 umol/L (60-110), lactate 4.8 mmol/L (under 2.0), high sensitivity troponin 480 ng/L (under 26)
data_table.Imaging: CTPA bilateral saddle embolus with RV/LV ratio 1.6, bedside echo dilated hypokinetic RV

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Catheter directed thrombolysis with reduced dose alteplase 24 mg over 12 hours plus IV heparin infusion
Therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg per kg twice daily alone with careful volume replacement and inotrope support
Immediate surgical embolectomy on cardiopulmonary bypass without first attempting systemic thrombolysis
Systemic alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours plus therapeutic unfractionated heparin infusion targeted to APTT
Insert an IVC filter first, then start therapeutic heparin infusion and reassess for tPA at 24 hours

subtopic_detail: pH 6.90 with severe hypokalaemia and altered conscious level
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 24-year-old woman with new type 1 diabetes presenting with 24 hours of vomiting and abdominal pain. Glasgow Coma Scale is 13. She is Kussmaul breathing at 32 per minute. Blood pressure is 96/58 with pulse 128. Weight is 60 kg. Venous blood gas pH is 6.90 with a bicarbonate of 4 and anion gap of 34. Plasma glucose is 32 mmol/L, potassium is 3.0, and creatinine 132. She has no urinary ketone strip but capillary ketones are 6.8.

Her initial 500 mL crystalloid bolus is running. You must set the initial insulin and potassium plan.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 100% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius, GCS 13
data_table.Bloods: sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), bicarbonate 4 mmol/L (22-32), creatinine 132 umol/L (45-90), glucose 32 mmol/L (3.5-8.0), pH 6.90, ketones 6.8 mmol/L (under 0.6), lactate 2.4 mmol/L (under 2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start dextrose 10 percent infusion and normal insulin infusion together to avoid rapid glucose fall over 2 hours
Start fixed rate insulin infusion at 0.1 units per kg per hour immediately alongside crystalloid resuscitation
Give IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol infusion over 30 minutes because pH is under 7.00 with cardiovascular risk
Give a subcutaneous rapid acting insulin bolus of 10 units and then commence oral fluids and delay IV insulin
Continue crystalloid resuscitation and replace potassium to over 3.5 mmol/L before starting insulin infusion

subtopic_detail: M1 middle cerebral artery occlusion at 4 hours from onset
stem:
You are the stroke registrar in a metropolitan ED reviewing a 68-year-old right-handed man who developed sudden left hemiparesis and neglect 4 hours ago on a family car trip. NIHSS is 18 with dense left arm weakness, forced right gaze deviation, and hemispatial neglect. He is on aspirin 100 mg for coronary disease. Non-contrast CT shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct; ASPECTS is 9. CT angiogram confirms a right M1 occlusion. CT perfusion shows a mismatch ratio of 2.1 with core 18 mL and penumbra 58 mL. He has no thrombolysis contraindications and weighs 82 kg.

Interventional neuroradiology is available in-house.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 86, blood pressure 168/94, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, GCS 14
data_table.Bloods: Hb 148 g/L (135-175), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 96 umol/L (60-110), INR 1.0, glucose 6.2 mmol/L (3.5-8.0)
data_table.Imaging: NCCT ASPECTS 9 no bleed, CTA right M1 occlusion, CTP core 18 mL penumbra 58 mL mismatch 2.1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: IV tenecteplase 0.25 mg per kg bolus now followed by endovascular thrombectomy for the M1 occlusion
Endovascular thrombectomy alone without IV thrombolysis because he is on aspirin already
IV thrombolysis only without thrombectomy because the CT ASPECTS score is 9 and core is small
Loading dose clopidogrel 300 mg plus aspirin 300 mg and admit to the stroke unit without reperfusion
Delay reperfusion until 24 hours to allow perfusion imaging repeat and reduce haemorrhagic transformation risk

subtopic_detail: Anterior STEMI with pulmonary oedema and hypotension after primary PCI
stem:
You are the coronary care unit registrar 4 hours after successful primary PCI to the LAD in a 62-year-old man with anterior STEMI. He is now hypotensive with blood pressure 78/52 despite noradrenaline at 0.4 mcg per kg per minute. He has bibasal crackles, JVP raised to angle, and cool peripheries. Echocardiogram shows LV ejection fraction 20 percent with anterior akinesis, moderate mitral regurgitation, and no mechanical complication. Lactate is 4.2. He is intubated and sedated. Cardiac output monitoring shows CI 1.6.

The interventional cardiologist has confirmed no residual coronary lesion.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 78/52 on noradrenaline 0.4, respiratory rate 22 ventilated, SpO2 92% on 60% FiO2, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 128 g/L (135-175), platelets 224 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 138 umol/L (60-110), lactate 4.2 mmol/L (under 2.0), high sensitivity troponin 42000 ng/L (under 26)
data_table.Imaging: echo LVEF 20% anterior akinesis moderate MR no VSD no tamponade, chest X-ray bilateral alveolar oedema

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in circulatory support?

options.text: Add dobutamine 5 mcg per kg per minute to noradrenaline and continue medical therapy with diuretics
Insert an Impella CP percutaneous LV assist device and wean noradrenaline as cardiac output improves
Give IV glyceryl trinitrate infusion at 20 mcg per minute to reduce afterload and improve pulmonary oedema now
Give IV levosimendan 0.1 mcg per kg per minute over 24 hours and continue current vasopressor support
Insert an intra-aortic balloon pump because IABP has proven mortality benefit in cardiogenic shock post-MI

subtopic_detail: Type 2 respiratory failure on maximal medical therapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar in ED with a 26-year-old woman with severe asthma who has not improved after continuous nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg, and IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes. She is diaphoretic, unable to speak in words, and has a silent chest. Peak flow was 90 L/min on arrival (best 420) and now cannot be recorded. Arterial gas 30 minutes into treatment shows pH 7.21, pCO2 68, pO2 62 on 15 L via non-rebreather. Heart rate is 148. She has a prior ICU admission for asthma.

The ICU consultant is at bedside for airway management.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 132/86, respiratory rate 42, SpO2 88% on 15 L NRB, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), lactate 4.6 mmol/L (under 2.0), pH 7.21, pCO2 68 mmHg (35-45), pO2 62 mmHg (80-100)
data_table.Imaging: chest X-ray hyperinflation no pneumothorax no consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: IV aminophylline 5 mg per kg loading dose over 20 minutes then continuous infusion 0.5 mg per kg per hour
Continuous BiPAP 12/6 cmH2O with pressure support titration and repeat gas in 30 minutes before intubation
Rapid sequence intubation with ketamine 1.5 mg per kg IV and rocuronium then lung protective ventilation
Repeat IV magnesium sulfate 2 g bolus and add second dose IV hydrocortisone before considering intubation
IV adrenaline infusion 0.05 mcg per kg per minute and continue nebulised beta-agonist without airway plan

subtopic_detail: Na 110 mmol/L with seizure and altered conscious state
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 74-year-old woman brought to ED after a witnessed 2 minute generalised seizure at home. She has been vomiting for 3 days and is on hydrochlorothiazide and citalopram. GCS is 12 now, no localising signs, no meningism. Sodium is 110, potassium 3.4, urea 6.4, creatinine 92, glucose 5.2. Serum osmolality is 240 and urine sodium 62. She is not clinically dehydrated. Airway is patent and BP is 122/74.

The intensivist is present and asks about immediate fluid strategy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 122/74, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, GCS 12
data_table.Bloods: sodium 110 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 6.4 mmol/L (2.5-8.0), creatinine 92 umol/L (45-90), glucose 5.2 mmol/L (3.5-8.0), serum osmolality 240 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 380 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 62 mmol/L
data_table.Imaging: CT brain unremarkable, chest X-ray clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate fluid management?

options.text: Give tolvaptan 15 mg orally now and start 0.9 percent saline at 100 mL per hour after loading dose is given
Start 0.9 percent saline infusion at 500 mL per hour and reassess sodium in 4 hours before other action
Fluid restrict to 800 mL per day and observe on the ward without giving any bolus of saline for 24 hours
Give 150 mL 3 percent saline bolus IV over 10 minutes and repeat once or twice to a maximum rise of 6 mmol/L in 24 hours
Give IV furosemide 40 mg and 0.9 percent saline together to remove free water and raise sodium concentration

subtopic_detail: Adult with subacute meningism and CSF lymphocytosis with low glucose
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 42-year-old man from a high TB prevalence country with 3 weeks of headache, fever, and progressive drowsiness. He has right sixth nerve palsy and mild neck stiffness. HIV serology is pending. CT brain shows basal meningeal enhancement and mild hydrocephalus with open ventricles. Lumbar puncture opening pressure is 32 cm CSF, protein 2.2 g/L, glucose 1.4 mmol/L with paired plasma 6.4, and 240 lymphocytes with 20 neutrophils. GeneXpert MTB/RIF positive on CSF is available in 2 hours.

He is stable but drowsy. You must initiate treatment now.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 124/78, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.1 degrees Celsius, GCS 13
data_table.Bloods: Hb 118 g/L (135-175), white cells 9.4 x10^9/L (4-11), sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 86 umol/L (60-110), ALT 32 U/L (5-40), CRP 68 mg/L (under 5)
data_table.Imaging: CT brain basal meningeal enhancement mild hydrocephalus, chest X-ray upper lobe infiltrates and small right hilar node

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start rifampicin and isoniazid only for 12 months with pyridoxine and defer pyrazinamide until sputum is available
Empirical ceftriaxone 2 g IV twice daily plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV 4 hourly awaiting culture data
Give IV aciclovir 10 mg per kg 8 hourly for possible herpes encephalitis and await MRI brain imaging
Start RIPE anti-tubercular therapy alone without corticosteroids because steroids risk TB dissemination
Start rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol plus IV dexamethasone 0.4 mg per kg per day tapered over 8 weeks

subtopic_detail: Persistent shock despite repeat IM adrenaline in a patient on beta-blocker
stem:
You are the medical registrar in ED with a 58-year-old man 15 minutes after peanut ingestion. He has facial swelling, widespread urticaria, wheeze, and stridor. He has received IM adrenaline 500 mcg twice at 5 minute intervals, IV fluid 2 litres crystalloid, IV hydrocortisone 200 mg, and IV chlorphenamine 10 mg, but remains hypotensive at 78/44 with pulse 62. He is on bisoprolol 5 mg for atrial fibrillation and rivaroxaban 20 mg. The airway is patent for now but stridor is worsening.

The anaesthetist is preparing for intubation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 62, blood pressure 78/44, respiratory rate 30, SpO2 90% on 15 L NRB, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, GCS 14
data_table.Bloods: Hb 138 g/L (135-175), platelets 220 x10^9/L (150-400), lactate 3.6 mmol/L (under 2.0), tryptase pending
data_table.Imaging: chest X-ray hyperinflation no oedema no pneumothorax

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start IV adrenaline infusion at 0.05 to 0.5 mcg per kg per minute and give IV glucagon 1 mg for beta-blocker effect
Continue further IM adrenaline every 5 minutes and add nebulised salbutamol without changing route or dose
Give IV noradrenaline 0.1 mcg per kg per minute as first line vasopressor instead of adrenaline in this case
Give IV hydrocortisone 500 mg further and repeat IV chlorphenamine 10 mg without additional vasopressor therapy
Give IV dopamine 5 mcg per kg per minute infusion and delay intubation because airway may improve with fluids

subtopic_detail: Wells score with age-adjusted D-dimer threshold
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 78-year-old woman with 24 hours of pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnoea. She had a total knee replacement 3 weeks ago and is mobilising with a frame at home. She has no haemoptysis, no leg swelling, and no history of malignancy. On examination she is haemodynamically stable with clear chest and no calf swelling or tenderness. Her chest X-ray is unremarkable. Her Wells score is 4.5 (surgery in last 4 weeks 1.5, PE as likely as alternative 3). An age-adjusted D-dimer using the 500 x age formula returns a value of 700 micrograms/L (age-adjusted cut-off 780).

Her creatinine is 92 micromol/L and eGFR is 62.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform CT pulmonary angiography as the Wells score of 4.5 places her in the PE-likely group requiring imaging
Discharge with reassurance because the age-adjusted D-dimer is below the cut-off for her age at 780 today value
CT pulmonary angiogram given the moderate Wells probability, notwithstanding the negative age-adjusted D-dimer today
Ventilation-perfusion scan first-line as the initial imaging modality due to her age and preserved renal function level
Bilateral lower limb Doppler ultrasound as a proxy investigation to avoid contrast exposure with age-related nephropathy risk

subtopic_detail: Membrane stabilisation and shift plus removal choices
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68-year-old man on haemodialysis who missed his last two sessions because he was interstate for a family bereavement. He presents with generalised weakness, palpitations, and nausea. He is on perindopril and spironolactone for cardiomyopathy. His observations show bradycardia and normotension. His ECG shows peaked T waves throughout, PR prolongation to 240 ms, and a QRS complex 130 ms without loss of P waves. Serum potassium is markedly raised. He has functioning tunnelled dialysis catheter access already in situ.

Nephrology is arranging urgent dialysis to run within the next 45 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 48, blood pressure 128/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.ECG: peaked T waves, PR 240 ms, QRS 130 ms, no loss of P waves, no arrhythmia
data_table.Bloods: potassium 7.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), sodium 138 mmol/L, urea 32 mmol/L, creatinine 720 micromol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, glucose 6.4 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: perindopril 10 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, carvedilol 6.25 mg BD

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Withhold treatment until formal potassium result is repeated to rule out haemolysis and dialysis is ready to commence
Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g stat with repeat 8 hourly while awaiting haemodialysis for potassium removal today
Nebulised salbutamol 10 mg alone with cessation of perindopril and spironolactone while awaiting the dialysis session
IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 10 minutes as first-line treatment for the wide complex and metabolic acidosis today
IV calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent solution followed by insulin-dextrose shift and immediate haemodialysis when available

subtopic_detail: Escalation to IV magnesium after inadequate response to nebulisers
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 24-year-old woman with known asthma presenting with a 6 hour deterioration despite home salbutamol every hour. She was hospitalised twice in the last year and takes budesonide-formoterol maintenance and reliever therapy. She is anxious, speaking in short phrases, and using accessory muscles. Peak expiratory flow is 40 percent of predicted. She has completed 20 minutes of back to back salbutamol and ipratropium via oxygen-driven nebuliser and received oral prednisolone 50 mg 30 minutes ago. Repeat observations show ongoing distress.

Her arterial blood gas shows a normal pCO2 which the intern reports as reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132, blood pressure 128/76, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 91% on 6 L Hudson, temperature 36.7
data_table.Chest: widespread expiratory wheeze with reduced air entry bilaterally, no focal signs
data_table.ABG: pH 7.38, pO2 68 mmHg, pCO2 40 mmHg (normal - concerning for exhaustion), HCO3 24 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue salbutamol nebulisers hourly and give a second dose of oral prednisolone 50 mg 4 hours later after further review
IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes and admit to critical care area with anaesthetic team stand by immediately
Non-invasive ventilation with BiPAP settings at IPAP 12 EPAP 6 as first-line escalation before IV therapy adjuncts
IV hydrocortisone 200 mg with repeat salbutamol nebuliser and discharge planning if PEF improves to above 60 percent
IV adrenaline 500 micrograms subcutaneously for severe bronchospasm as first line escalation for acute presentation today

subtopic: GI bleed on direct oral anticoagulant
subtopic_detail: Reversal choice for apixaban with acute upper GI bleed
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 72-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation on apixaban 5 mg twice daily for stroke prevention. She presents with haematemesis of around 500 mL in the last 4 hours and 2 melaena stools. She last took apixaban this morning 2 hours ago. She has a history of gastric ulcer 5 years ago on aspirin, which is now ceased. Her observations show tachycardia and borderline blood pressure. Endoscopy will be available in 3 hours. Her creatinine is 108 micromol/L and eGFR is 52.

Her bloods show a haemoglobin drop from 118 to 92 g/L since baseline.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 96/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Bloods: haemoglobin 92 g/L (baseline 118), platelets 202 x10^9/L, INR 1.2, urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L
data_table.Medications: apixaban 5 mg BD (last dose 2 hours ago), no aspirin
data_table.Access: two large bore IVs, cross-match 4 units sent, PPI infusion started

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal agent choice?

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 4 units and cryoprecipitate 10 units as reversal of the anticoagulant effect prior to the endoscopy
Andexanet alfa (if available) or 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 50 units per kg with activated charcoal 50 g stat
IV vitamin K 10 mg with a repeat INR in 6 hours before considering endoscopic intervention this evening in this patient
IV idarucizumab 5 g given as two 2.5 g doses with a second cross match sample and endoscopy planning within 2 hours
IV tranexamic acid 1 g bolus alone as reversal of the direct oral anticoagulant with rapid onset of therapeutic effect

subtopic_detail: Second-line agent choice after benzodiazepine failure
stem:
You are the emergency medical registrar reviewing a 42-year-old man with known focal epilepsy on levetiracetam 1500 mg twice daily. He was brought in with a generalised tonic-clonic seizure that has persisted for 12 minutes despite two 10 mg IV midazolam boluses given by paramedics 5 and 10 minutes ago. He continues to seize actively on arrival. He has no known intracranial pathology on prior MRI. Bedside blood glucose is normal. There is no head trauma or intoxication history.

The anaesthetic registrar is 5 minutes away and preparing for possible intubation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 138, blood pressure 152/94, respiratory rate 20 with obstructive pattern, SpO2 92% on 15 L Hudson, temperature 37.6
data_table.Bedside tests: glucose 5.6 mmol/L, no head trauma, IV access secured, ECG normal sinus
data_table.Medications: levetiracetam 1500 mg BD (last dose 6 hours ago), no other current medication
data_table.Prior treatment: midazolam 10 mg IV x 2 at 5 and 10 minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate second-line agent?

options.text: IV thiopental 5 mg per kg induction with immediate intubation for airway protection and prolonged sedation for the seizure
IV phenytoin 18 mg per kg loading dose over 30 minutes with continuous cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia and hypotension
IV midazolam infusion 0.1 mg per kg per hour titrated to seizure cessation with intubation for airway protection needs
IV levetiracetam 60 mg per kg loading dose maximum 4500 mg given over 10 minutes with cardiac monitoring during infusion
IV magnesium sulfate 4 g over 15 minutes as second line agent to address the ongoing seizure activity in this patient

subtopic_detail: Chloride burden with renal impairment during first 24 hours
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 34-year-old man with type 1 diabetes who presents with 24 hours of vomiting, polyuria, and altered sensorium. He is dehydrated and Kussmaul breathing. His bedside glucose is high and gas confirms severe metabolic acidosis with a large anion gap. The intern has already given 1 L of 0.9 percent saline over 30 minutes. Serum potassium came back at 3.4 mmol/L. He has usually good renal function; today creatinine has risen slightly with a modest calculated eGFR reduction. His fluid balance and hourly urine output monitoring is being organised.

The insulin infusion has not yet been commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 106/68, respiratory rate 32 Kussmaul, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9, GCS 13
data_table.Bloods: glucose 32 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, chloride 108 mmol/L, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L (baseline 78), pH 6.98, ketones 6.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next fluid and electrolyte step?

options.text: Give 1 L Hartmann's solution with 20 mmol potassium chloride over 60 minutes before commencing IV insulin infusion therapy
Commence IV insulin infusion 0.1 units per kg per hour before further potassium or fluid changes as the priority now
Give another litre of 0.9 percent saline as fluid with 10 mmol potassium chloride and start insulin infusion 0.05 units per kg per hour
Give IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 30 minutes given the severe acidosis of pH 6.98 as a first line to correct pH now
Give 5 percent dextrose 1 L with 40 mmol potassium chloride over 4 hours as fluid choice for the ongoing management now

subtopic_detail: Secondary adrenal insufficiency during illness with atypical timing
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 62-year-old man with metastatic melanoma on combination ipilimumab and nivolumab, cycle 3, day 21. He presents with 5 days of worsening lethargy, nausea, vomiting, and postural dizziness. Today he cannot stand without near-syncope. He denies fever or diarrhoea. He is not on regular steroids. His bloods show marked hyponatraemia with normal potassium and hypoglycaemia. Random morning cortisol is markedly low (35 nmol/L) and ACTH is not elevated. TSH is low with low free T4.

He collapses while being transferred from ED trolley to ward bed.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128 supine, 148 sitting, blood pressure 88/54 supine, 68/40 sitting, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.5
data_table.Bloods: sodium 118 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, glucose 2.6 mmol/L, urea 8.4 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L, cortisol 35 nmol/L (>500 stress-normal), ACTH 2 pmol/L (2-11 normal, low here), TSH 0.4 mIU/L, free T4 8 pmol/L
data_table.Medications: combination ipilimumab plus nivolumab (day 21 of cycle 3), paracetamol PRN
data_table.Prior: no diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency, no chronic steroids

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, then 100 mg 6 hourly, plus 5 percent dextrose in 0.9 percent saline resuscitation
IV levothyroxine 500 micrograms loading dose given the low TSH and low free T4 as first line prior to any steroid
IV normal saline 2 L over 4 hours with hypertonic saline 3 percent for the hyponatraemia and monitoring before steroid
IV dexamethasone 8 mg alone as steroid replacement with 0.9 percent saline resuscitation and endocrine review tomorrow
Ceasing checkpoint inhibitor therapy alone with observation on cardiac monitor and endocrine referral within 24 hours

subtopic: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state with mixed DKA features
subtopic_detail: Fluid strategy when osmolality and ketosis both present
stem:
You are the intensive care registrar reviewing a 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin and empagliflozin who was found by his wife drowsy and confused. He had been unwell with a chest infection for 5 days, with reduced oral intake. On arrival his glucose is markedly high with an elevated calculated osmolality; he also has mild ketosis and a bicarbonate at the lower end of normal with a raised anion gap. His creatinine is significantly elevated over baseline. He is severely dehydrated with tachycardia and hypotension. GCS is 12.

He has a history of ischaemic heart disease and moderate left ventricular systolic dysfunction.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 26 mildly Kussmaul, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.6, GCS 12
data_table.Bloods: glucose 44 mmol/L, sodium 152 mmol/L (measured; corrected 160), potassium 4.6 mmol/L, urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 220 micromol/L (baseline 88), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, ketones 3.2 mmol/L, pH 7.28, calculated osmolality 348 mmol/kg
data_table.Medications: metformin, empagliflozin, atorvastatin, perindopril, bisoprolol, aspirin
data_table.Estimated fluid deficit: 8-10 L based on osmolar picture and dehydration signs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid strategy?

options.text: IV 5 percent dextrose 1 L with insulin 0.1 units per kg per hour as an initial approach because ketones are present now
IV 0.9 percent saline 2 L over 30 minutes with insulin infusion 0.1 units per kg per hour as standard DKA fluid strategy today
IV 0.45 percent saline 2 L over 60 minutes as the primary resuscitation fluid to correct hyperosmolality first now today
IV 0.9 percent saline 1 L over 60 minutes with insulin infusion 0.05 units per kg per hour and euglycaemic DKA precautions applied
Hartmann's solution 2 L over 60 minutes with immediate insulin bolus of 0.15 units per kg to bring glucose down rapidly

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic and dexamethasone timing before lumbar puncture
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department assessing a 24-year-old university student brought in by her housemates after two days of headache, fever and increasing confusion this morning. She has never been unwell before and takes no regular medications. On arrival she is drowsy but rousable. There is meningism on examination and a purpuric rash is developing on her lower legs.

She has had one seizure witnessed by paramedics 20 minutes ago that self-terminated within a minute.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 96% on 6 L Hudson, temperature 39.4
data_table.Neurological: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), no focal deficit, neck stiffness present, photophobia
data_table.Skin: spreading non-blanching purpura on lower legs and forearms
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): white cells 18 x10^9/L, platelets 128 x10^9/L, CRP 220 mg/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L, INR 1.4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Perform urgent lumbar puncture before any antibiotic administration to preserve CSF culture yield and guide targeted therapy in the current clinical setting
Give IV mannitol 1 g/kg over 30 minutes for raised intracranial pressure and intubate to protect airway before considering antibiotic therapy
Commence oral amoxicillin 1 g eight-hourly and admit to the medical ward for observation while awaiting CT and LP results tomorrow morning
Empirically start intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours alone for suspected herpes simplex encephalitis and defer bacterial cover until CSF results are available
Administer IV dexamethasone 10 mg immediately followed by IV ceftriaxone 2 g and benzylpenicillin 2.4 g (or replace with vancomycin if pneumococcal resistance concerns), then proceed

subtopic_detail: Recognising surgical urgency in an ostensibly simple cellulitis
stem:
You are the emergency department medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes admitted 12 hours ago with left leg redness and fever, treated as cellulitis with IV flucloxacillin. Overnight his pain has escalated beyond what the erythematous area would suggest and he is now systemically unwell. On examination the erythema has extended by more than a hand-breadth and the skin is dusky with a small purple bulla forming.

His leg is exquisitely tender to light touch, with pain out of proportion to the surface findings.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132, blood pressure 98/62, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal cannula, temperature 39.1
data_table.Left leg: erythema extending from foot to mid-thigh with poorly defined margins, dusky central area, single purple bulla 2 cm, crepitus not palpable, exquisitely tender
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): white cells 22 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 108 g/L (135-175), sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 90), CRP 340 mg/L, glucose 18 mmol/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L
data_table.Diabetes: HbA1c 92 mmol/mol at last GP visit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue IV flucloxacillin monotherapy, mark the erythematous margin with a skin pen, and reassess in 6 hours for extension before considering escalation
Escalate to IV meropenem 1 g eight-hourly plus IV clindamycin 600 mg eight-hourly plus IV vancomycin, aggressive resuscitation, and immediate surgical review for emergency debridement
Order urgent MRI of the leg to confirm fascial involvement before deciding on operative management to avoid unnecessary debridement in the current clinical setting
Commence hyperbaric oxygen therapy as first-line adjunctive treatment before surgical intervention to arrest tissue necrosis via oxygen delivery
Add IV metronidazole 500 mg eight-hourly to flucloxacillin, admit to the ward for continued observation without transfer to a surgical unit

subtopic_detail: Sick-day hydrocortisone dosing in a patient with primary adrenal insufficiency
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department reviewing a 45-year-old woman with known Addison's disease on hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking, 10 mg at midday, and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily. She has had 24 hours of vomiting from viral gastroenteritis with inability to tolerate oral hydrocortisone. She is drowsy and cool peripherally. She reports her sick-day plan requires her to double her hydrocortisone but she could not keep the tablets down.

Her MedicAlert bracelet confirms the diagnosis.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 82/48, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 12.4 mmol/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, cortisol pending, ACTH pending
data_table.Perfusion: capillary refill 4 seconds, cool peripheries, dry mucosa
data_table.Established diagnosis: primary adrenal insufficiency, on stable replacement for 8 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give IV dexamethasone 4 mg stat because it does not interfere with a subsequent short synacthen test that will confirm the diagnosis
Give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 50 mg every 6 hours or 200 mg per 24 hours infusion, 1 L 0.9 percent saline over 30 minutes
Give IV fludrocortisone 100 micrograms IM stat and IV normal saline; withhold hydrocortisone until oral tolerance resumes to prevent Cushingoid effects
Give oral hydrocortisone 40 mg dispersed in water via nasogastric tube and 1 L 0.9 percent saline over 4 hours in the current clinical setting
Commence peripheral noradrenaline infusion at 8 micrograms/min for shock and defer glucocorticoid replacement until cardiovascular stability is achieved

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic choice and IV/oral switch in an admitted adult
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department reviewing a 38-year-old woman with 24 hours of right loin pain, rigors, and dysuria for three days. She has no known drug allergy and is not pregnant. She has never had a UTI before and has no urological history. She reports one episode of vomiting on arrival.

She is systemically unwell but haemodynamically stable after 1 L of 0.9 percent saline.

data_table.Vital signs after 1 L saline: pulse 108, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Right loin: tenderness on percussion, no palpable mass
data_table.Urinalysis: leucocytes 4+, nitrites positive, blood 2+, protein trace
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): white cells 16.4 x10^9/L, CRP 148 mg/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L (baseline unknown), lactate 2.1 mmol/L
data_table.Local antibiogram: no recent urinary Enterobacterales resistance concerns; local first-line remains gentamicin plus amoxicillin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g eight-hourly as broad-spectrum empirical cover for likely ESBL Enterobacterales in the current clinical setting under standard AU management
IV ciprofloxacin 400 mg 12-hourly as monotherapy empirical treatment with oral switch to ciprofloxacin 500 mg 12-hourly at 48 hours to complete 7 days total
Oral trimethoprim 300 mg once daily for 7 days and discharge home with GP follow-up in 48 hours in the current clinical setting under standard AU management
IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily plus IV amoxicillin 2 g six-hourly, with switch to oral cefalexin or amoxicillin-clavulanate based on susceptibility in 24-48 hours to complete 10-14 days total
IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily monotherapy for 10 days without gentamicin, given the risk of aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity in acute pyelonephritis in the current clinical setting

subtopic_detail: Preoperative alpha-blockade before beta-blockade sequence
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 44-year-old man in the endocrine outpatient clinic three weeks after admission for hypertensive crisis with headache and diaphoresis. His 24 hour urinary fractionated metanephrines returned at seven times upper limit of normal. MIBG imaging localises a 5 cm right adrenal mass. Surgery is scheduled in six weeks. He is not currently on any antihypertensive therapy.

His clinic BP today is 168/102 and he asks about starting treatment before the operation.

data_table.Vital signs today: pulse 92, blood pressure 168/102, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Investigations: 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines 7x ULN, MIBG-positive right 5 cm adrenal mass
data_table.Cardiovascular: no chest pain, no cardiac history, ECG sinus rhythm, no LVH

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Commence oral phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily titrated up over 2 weeks with liberal salt and fluid intake, then add propranolol 20 mg three times daily only after alpha-blockade is established
Commence oral atenolol 50 mg daily as first-line therapy to control the tachycardia and hypertension, then add doxazosin 4 mg daily one week before surgery
Commence oral amlodipine 5 mg daily and no other antihypertensive, deferring alpha and beta blockade until the day before surgery to avoid symptomatic hypotension
Commence oral perindopril 5 mg daily and salt restriction as standard hypertension management until surgical review in the current clinical setting
Commence oral labetalol 200 mg twice daily as combined alpha and beta blockade in a single agent to simplify preoperative preparation in the current clinical setting

subtopic_detail: Choosing between IVIG and plasmapheresis in a rapidly deteriorating patient
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 52-year-old woman with a two-year history of myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine 60 mg five times daily and prednisolone 20 mg daily. She presented 12 hours ago with rapid worsening bulbar and respiratory weakness after starting azithromycin two days earlier for a chest infection. Her vital capacity has fallen from an admission 2.1 L to 1.2 L over the last four hours. Negative inspiratory pressure is now -20 cmH2O.

She has not previously required plasmapheresis or IVIG.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 132/82, respiratory rate 26 shallow, SpO2 96% on 6 L Hudson, temperature 37.4
data_table.Bulbar: dysarthria worsening, weak cough, drooling of saliva, unable to swallow reliably
data_table.Respiratory function: vital capacity 1.2 L (baseline 3.4 L; alarm threshold usually <15 mL/kg or 1 L; NIP -20 cmH2O with -30 as threshold)
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): white cells 12 x10^9/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, urea 6.8 mmol/L, IgA level pending
data_table.Chest X-ray: right lower lobe consolidation being treated
data_table.Precipitant: azithromycin recently commenced (aminoglycoside/macrolide class known to worsen myasthenia)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Admit to intensive care, cease azithromycin, prepare for intubation given falling vital capacity, start intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days
Double the pyridostigmine dose to 120 mg every 4 hours to maximise cholinergic transmission before deciding on advanced therapies
Give IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days as high-dose pulse steroid therapy and defer IVIG or plasmapheresis to see if steroid response occurs first
Give a single IV dose of edrophonium 10 mg to differentiate cholinergic crisis from myasthenic crisis before further therapy
Administer intramuscular neostigmine 1.5 mg six-hourly as an alternative to pyridostigmine while awaiting immunotherapy

subtopic_detail: Stanford classification and immediate management divergence
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department reviewing a 62-year-old man with sudden onset tearing interscapular chest pain radiating to the back that woke him from sleep 90 minutes ago. He has a background of hypertension on irbesartan and smokes 30 pack years. A CT aortogram has just returned and shows a dissection flap starting at the ascending aorta and extending distally through the arch and descending thoracic aorta to the level of the diaphragm. There is no pericardial effusion or ischaemic complication.

He has a mild new murmur of aortic regurgitation and his left brachial pulse is diminished compared with the right.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 168/98 (left arm 142/86), respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% on 4 L nasal cannula, temperature 36.9
data_table.CT aortogram: dissection flap ascending aorta through arch and descending thoracic aorta to diaphragm; no pericardial effusion; no coronary involvement; no visceral ischaemia; false lumen patent
data_table.Cardiovascular: new soft early diastolic murmur, left brachial pulse diminished, no tamponade
data_table.Bloods: troponin negative, D-dimer elevated, creatinine 92 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Admit to the coronary care unit for medical management with IV labetalol only, and interval outpatient thoracic surgery review in 4 weeks given absence of pericardial effusion
IV nitroprusside infusion titrated to systolic blood pressure 100 to 120 mmHg as initial management, without prior beta-blockade to allow for rapid titration
IV heparin infusion for suspected pulmonary embolism given the pleuritic chest pain and mediastinal widening on chest radiograph in the current clinical setting
IV labetalol infusion titrated to target heart rate 60 to 80 and systolic blood pressure 100 to 120 mmHg, IV opioid analgesia, and immediate cardiothoracic surgical referral for open aortic repair
Endovascular thoracic aortic stenting via femoral access as first-line intervention for a dissection extending into the descending aorta in the current clinical setting
